Title: Would Your Employees Join a Fake Anthropic AI Preview?
Context: In other campaigns, threat actors have abused non-AI, trusted services like link shorteners or cloud collaboration platforms as the first link in a phishing campaign to avoid...
Full Text:
By: Intelligence Team, Jacob Malimban

Since September 2026, threat actors have been sending emails that appear to be an invitation to a private Anthropic AI meeting, but are actually attempts to steal Google and Microsoft login credentials. Exclusive access to new AI technology is valuable to many organizations, which is why threat actors use it as a lure in their phishing emails.

Risks to the organization from this campaign include threat actors compromising a sensitive account, accessing the account’s sensitive documents (e.g. proprietary marketing material), and using the compromised account as an initial vector to further infiltrate the organization. Employees must stay vigilant, as these phishing emails bypass current email security technologies due to the abuse of legitimate tools like URL shorteners and CAPTCHAs.

Cofense Intelligence consolidates campaign data, including indicators of compromise (IOCs) such as malicious web addresses, phishing email content, and broader campaign context, into Active Threat Reports (ATRs), providing a comprehensive view of identified threats. ATRs contain the full infection chain from the initial phishing link to the final malware file or credential phishing resource. If one ATR IOC appears in the organization, cybersecurity professionals can read the ATR to understand the phishing attack’s impact and mitigations. Each ATR has been curated by a human analyst. This human-vetted intelligence provides context and the campaign information necessary to mitigate future phishing attacks. For this private Anthropic AI preview campaign, actionable intelligence can be found in ATRs 423868, 423866, and 423475.

Key Points

The campaign contains a tantalizing, private offer to preview Anthropic AI technology, which may be enough for employees to click before inspecting the email.

The video teleconference software GoTo Webinar, which is used to send legitimate meeting emails and is usually not blocked by email security technologies, was abused to send a threat actor’s URL instead.

The URL shortener zpr[.]io, which turns long URLs into short links, has been abused to help these phishing emails bypass current email security technologies.

CAPTCHAs, which are tests that confirm a real human is visiting the website, are similarly abused to prevent automated analysis.

Threat actors use subdomains and dashes (-) to obfuscate the malicious URL.

Step 1: The Invitation Email

Figure 1: Anthropic meeting invitation email used in credential phishing (ATR 423475).

Emails in this campaign claim to be an exclusive invitation to see Anthropic’s new AI tool. Many organizations are deciding how AI fits into their business, so a private preview would be very valuable if the email were real. As developments in AI continue to dominate the news cycle, getting a private preview of advancements in Anthropic’s AI is an effective phishing lure.

The phishing email appears to be an abuse of the legitimate GoTo Webinar service. The email sender address appears to be customercare@gotowebinar[.]com. Threat actors have previously abused that email address and GoTo Webinar’s free trial in 2020. The email also contains a footer with GoTo Webinar branding.

The text in the email contains no obvious spelling errors. The email sender name, however, reads “Austin from nthropic” with the “A” missing from Anthropic. Although this is a small misspelling, it is still a useful warning sign.

The link in the email appears to be generated by Zapier’s URL shortener service. Zapier is a legitimate business process automation company, and their URL Shortener is designed to work with Claude, ChatGPT, and other MCP-compatible AI. Unfortunately, this tool has been abused by threat actors during this Anthropic AI Preview campaign. In other campaigns, threat actors have abused non-AI, trusted services like link shorteners or cloud collaboration platforms as the first link in a phishing campaign to avoid being blocked by email security technologies.

Step 2: The First Checkpoint

Figure 2: Cloudflare CAPTCHA page to hinder automated analysis (ATR 423868).

If the phishing email link is clicked, a CAPTCHA page appears. This Cloudflare CAPTCHA must be completed before the phishing content is shown. This CAPTCHA is the first of two checkpoints that help threat actors block automated scans of their website. Because CAPTCHAs are common on legitimate websites, phishing recipients may believe all is well and everything is secure because of the CAPTCHA.

Step 3: The Fake Meeting Page

Figure 3: Zoom-spoofing page with Anthropic meeting information (ATR 423475).

After completing the CAPTCHA, a Zoom-spoofing meeting invitation page appears. This brand does not match the GoTo Webinar branding from the email. The page’s Zoom branding is consistent with the “zoom” in the malicious domain, us968web-zoom[.]us.

If the phishing recipient wants to attend the “meeting”, they need to register for the event. They are prompted to register with their work email. Credential phishing occurs when the user clicks on either “Continue with Google” or “Continue with Microsoft”.

Step 4: The Second Checkpoint

Figure 4: Custom CAPTCHA page to further hinder automated analysis (ATR 423475).

After clicking “Continue with Google” or “Continue with Microsoft”, another CAPTCHA page appears. This CAPTCHA requires a sliding motion to “unlock” the page. This custom CAPTCHA also appears to be good at detecting and blocking analysis from the most popular VPN services, scanners, Tor browser, and other tools used by defenders.

Because the phishing attack has two distinct CAPTCHAs, automated analysis tools may not be able to follow every step in the credential phishing attack.

Step 5A: The Fake Google Login Page

Figure 5: Google credential phishing page after custom CAPTCHA (ATR 423866).

If “Continue with Google” is clicked and the CAPTCHA is completed, the Google credential phishing page appears. Currently, the Google credential phishing page only captures usernames. It is likely that the page is misconfigured as it does not prompt for a password. After credentials are submitted, the browser does not redirect to the real Google login page, nor does a fake confirmation appear.

Not only is the phishing page remarkably similar to the legitimate Google login page, but the subdomain is also tricky. Employees who quickly read goo[.]gle-access-eventregister[.]icu might not recognize that the URL is not Google.

Step 5B: The Fake Microsoft Login Page

Figure 6: Microsoft credential phishing page after custom CAPTCHA (ATR 423475).

If instead of clicking on “Continue with Google”, the user clicked “Continue with Microsoft”, the Microsoft credential phishing page would load. Just like the previous Google Credential Phishing section, the CAPTCHA must be completed (Figure 4) before the phishing content is shown. Unlike the Google credential phishing page, the Microsoft version captures both the username and password. After credentials are submitted, the browser does not redirect to the real Microsoft login page, nor does a fake confirmation appear.

The Microsoft phishing page mimics the real Microsoft login page well. It also has a tricky subdomain, where office[.]com-access-sharepoint[.]com mimics the real office[.]com or sharepoint[.]com domain. Entering credentials into this page exfiltrates them to the threat actor.

Conclusion

This report covers the private Anthropic AI Preview campaign that uses a fake invitation lure, multiple CAPTCHAs, and Google and Microsoft login page replicas. The campaign was very likely designed by threat actors to bypass current email security technologies and tools used by defenders. Once the employee has reached the credential phishing page, they may not be looking for warning signs anymore. The Google credential phishing page only targets usernames, whereas the Microsoft credential phishing page asks for both the username and password. Stolen credentials give threat actors access to a trusted account, the emails stored in it, and a foothold for future attacks against the organization.

Mitigations

Check if the brand remains consistent from the email to a login page. Although organizations can use services like GoTo Webinar to send meetings on their behalf, a GoTo Webinar email is unlikely to redirect to a Zoom event registration page. Searching for small inconsistencies can help identify an email as part of a phishing campaign.

Remind employees that both the URL and domain determine whether a login page is legitimate. Although the logos and design of the page may look correct, threat actors are skilled at mimicry especially now with the use of AI. Note that the URL in the email might not be the same URL as the login page due to URL redirects.

Use Cofense Vision. Vision AI can cluster structurally related messages even when threat actors rotate senders, subjects, URLs, and page elements.

Invest in human-vetted threat intelligence to complement automated feeds. Automated systems are fast but cannot always tell the difference between a legitimate tool being used by IT and the same tool being abused by threat actors, and human analysis adds the context and confidence that AI-based speed cannot provide.

To learn how Cofense combines AI-driven detection, human-vetted threat intelligence, and rapid remediation to identify and stop sophisticated phishing attacks that bypass traditional security defenses, visit cofense.com/platform.

Title: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries
Context: Attackers have used fake ChatGPT and Claude desktop applications hosted on GitHub to distribute a malware chain that abuses legitimate signed binaries to evade security protections
Full Text:
Attackers have used fake ChatGPT and Claude desktop applications hosted on GitHub to distribute a malware chain that abuses legitimate signed binaries to evade security protections.

In research published October 27, Check Point said it had tracked the campaign, which it calls Yoba, for two months, though an earlier variant posing as the Cursor coding agent appeared in early June. The fake projects impersonated artificial intelligence (AI) applications including GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus.

Their releases sat in GitHub repositories with GitHub Pages landing pages, and some of the repositories appeared among Google’s top results, most likely through search engine optimization (SEO) poisoning.

Yoba Uses Signed Binaries to Hide Malicious Components

The fake applications bundled legitimate signed OpenAI and Anthropic executables with a malicious dynamic link library (DLL). Check Point found that the signed Setup.exe files loaded the malicious component through DLL sideloading, a technique often used to bypass security protections.

The malicious DLL, dubbed YobaDropper, ran several checks before deploying a second-stage loader, including the name of its host process and whether it had administrator privileges.

It also checked keyboard layouts to avoid machines in Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries other than Ukraine and used lengthy sleeps to frustrate automated analysis. Check Point said the actor showed indicators suggesting Russian origins.

The dropper then created a directory under ProgramData, copied a legitimate Windows executable into it and used Scheduled Tasks to establish persistence, with a task running under the Local System account and disguised as a Microsoft task.

Read more on fake AI tools spreading malware: Attackers Combine ChatGPT Feature Abuse With ClickFix to Deliver Trojan Malware

YobaLoader Uses Telegram and DNS to Fetch Payloads

The second-stage YobaLoader used Telegram and encrypted Domain Name System (DNS) lookups, known as DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH), to obtain instructions without dedicated command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, according to Check Point.

It took an image from a Telegram channel and used data from it to generate domains through a domain generation algorithm.

It then queried Google’s DoH service for encrypted data stored in DNS records, which was cryptographically validated before the loader retrieved and decrypted the next-stage payload.

Check Point advised organizations to be cautious when installing AI applications from unverified repositories and to restrict the execution of software from unknown sources.

The observed payload was an XMRig cryptominer, but the researchers said YobaLoader is a generic loader, so future waves could deliver other executable or PowerShell payloads.

In-app surveys capture feedback

In-app surveys add the team's own perspective on that work. The default questions focus on value: the most valuable thing someone has done with Claude recently, how Claude changed the time that work took, which use of Claude a teammate should copy, and, if the team lost access tomorrow, what would break or slow down first. Admins can customize or remove questions and choose who receives a survey, when it runs, and where it appears. Members see it as a short card after a reply in the tool they’re already working in.

Responses appear on the survey page as they arrive, and admins can export them to a spreadsheet. In-app surveys can now be enabled for organizations that use customer-managed encryption keys, and for organizations that set one retention period for all data, surveys and their responses are deleted on that schedule.

Pooled group budgets put spend where the work happens

Pooled group budgets give a group one shared monthly budget, so people who use Claude heavily are less likely to hit an individual limit early in the month while others leave budget unspent. Member limits still work as a guardrail against unusually high individual use. Every request counts against both, and a member stops at whichever runs out first. When someone hits a limit, they can request more from inside Claude, and the request goes to admins for review. The setup suggests an amount based on the group's recent usage, and admins with billing permissions receive email alerts at 50%, 75%, 95%, and 100% of a budget.

Getting started

Smart reports, in-app surveys, and pooled group budgets are generally available today for Claude Enterprise. Title: IDC brings Quanta into Claude and adopts Claude across the company
Context: IDC Research (IDC), a global leader in technology intelligence for more than 60 years, worked with Anthropic to bring IDC Quanta into Claude, available to IDC customers today
Full Text:
IDC Research (IDC), a global leader in technology intelligence for more than 60 years, worked with Anthropic to bring IDC Quanta into Claude, available to IDC customers today. IDC Quanta gives customers access to IDC’s trusted and validated forecasts, market data, research, and more, and now, they can ask questions in Claude to get answers enriched with IDC’s insights in minutes. IDC has also rolled Claude out across the company, where teams use it every day.

Applying market research has traditionally meant reading through long reports to get to the answers a customer needs, such as a vendor shortlist or a competitive brief. Now, an IDC customer describes the market, strategy, or purchase they're working on, and the IDC Quanta MCP connector for Claude returns finished analysis built on IDC's trusted forecasts and data.

What customers can do with IDC Quanta in Claude

IDC Quanta, an AI-powered technology intelligence platform that helps customers do better work, faster, with credible, verified intelligence from IDC’s proprietary data and research. In Claude, IDC Quanta enables customers to benchmark performance, size markets, choose vendors, and shape strategy. It’s as simple as a customer describing the question they're working on, and Claude answering it using IDC's intelligence.

The questions that users ask vary by role, but they tend to look like this:

Competitive briefs: A corporate strategy lead asks Claude for a competitor brief. Claude returns the competitor’s positioning, market share, product capabilities, and recent acquisitions, cited to IDC's research. A job that used to take a day’s worth of research is complete in minutes.

Vendor shortlists: A CIO evaluating procurement software asks Claude which vendors are the best fit based on her existing architecture and unique business requirements. Claude returns the top three by IDC's procurement database and MarketScape research as an Excel scorecard, ready for the evaluation team to act on.

Analysis of their own numbers: A CFO uploads next year's IT budget, and asks how it compares to IDC's forecast. Claude returns where the two differ, and by how much, while updated data stays private to the customer.

IDC Quanta works wherever the customer already uses Claude, including the Claude app on desktop and mobile, Cowork, and the Microsoft Office add-ins. It gives Claude the same data and definitions an IDC analyst works from, so a market share or growth rate matches what IDC would publish, and each answer cites the IDC document or dataset it came from.

How IDC uses Claude internally

IDC has also put Claude to work across the company, where its engineers, product, marketing and sales teams are using it daily to build, plan, and sell. A clear example of the difference it's making is in engineering: IDC's engineers rebuilt the internal data repository its analysts use for research in three weeks instead of an estimated three months, and since they began using Claude Code for testing, bugs in the code they ship have come down significantly.

Engineering was the first team to adopt Claude, and the rest of the company has followed. Here's how they're using it:

Building and testing software: Product managers use Claude Code to build working prototypes before engineering starts, which has cut the time it takes a feature to reach engineering from months to weeks. Engineers use it to run tests in parallel, and a code review that once filled five days is done in about 30 minutes.

Planning and strategy: Product teams give Cowork their research and internal files, and it writes the first draft of the plan. Planning sprints that took three weeks now take three days. Writing a new test to check that code works now takes about 20 minutes, down from days.

Optimizing sales: IDC's sales team runs a tool built with Claude that reads an export from the company's CRM. In minutes, it tells each rep which of their deals have stalled and which are worth chasing.

Producing marketing content: IDC's content marketing team built an assistant in Claude to draft much of its marketing content. It optimizes the content for search and AI answer engines (SEO/AEO), and checks it against buyer personas and IDC's own research. From there, the team edits, proofs, and publishes the work, publishing content faster than it could on its own

“Assessing the impact of a competitor’s acquisition used to mean a market intelligence professional spending hours pulling multiple reports, synthesizing the findings, and turning them into an executive-ready brief. Now, they can open Claude, ask what that acquisition means for their business, and get a board-ready analysis in minutes, grounded in IDC’s research and more than 15 billion data points,” said Lorenzo Larini, CEO, IDC. “We brought IDC Quanta into Claude because that’s where many of our customers already work, giving them a faster, more intuitive way to put IDC’s trusted data and research to work.”

“IDC has spent 60 years helping leaders make better technology decisions, and now it’s using Claude to rethink how its teams work and how it delivers value to its customers,” said Paul Smith, Chief Commercial Officer, Anthropic.

Getting started

IDC Quanta customers who use Claude can add the IDC Quanta connector from within Claude. Others can contact IDC or book a demo. To learn more about Claude for Enterprise, visit anthropic.com/enterprise.

Title: Tricks from the Past deployed via signed ChatGPT and Claude binaries
Context: Key Points Check Point Research discovered a campaign we track as Yoba where attackers abuse the popularity of AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, creating fake GitHub projects...
Full Text:
Key Points

Check Point Research discovered a campaign we track as Yoba where attackers abuse the popularity of AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, creating fake GitHub projects that pretend to be desktop applications like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus.

The malware is placed next to legitimate, signed executables from OpenAI and Anthropic so it can be loaded indirectly, a technique commonly known as DLL sideloading, which is often used to bypass security protections.

This campaign demonstrates strong operational security (OPSEC) by avoiding dedicated command-and-control (C2) infrastructure and instead relying on Telegram, Tor, Catbox, and DNS over HTTPS (DoH).

The actor behind the campaign shows indicators that suggest Russian origins and appears to operate primarily in the UTC-4 time zone.

Introduction

Over the past two months, we have been tracking a campaign that abuses the popularity of AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude to spread a custom malware chain we call Yoba. The attackers use fake GitHub projects that pretend to be AI desktop applications like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus. These projects look convincing and use real GitHub infrastructure, which helps them appear legitimate to potential victims. The website exhibits search-targeted content and suspicious installer-delivery tactics consistent with an SEO-poisoning lure.

Inside the installers, there is a malicious component we refer to as the YobaDropper. This dropper includes another component, the YobaLoader, which is responsible for contacting attacker-controlled infrastructure and fetching the final payload. In this report, we describe how victims are lured to these fake projects, how the YobaDropper and YobaLoader work together, and how the attackers ultimately use this chain to run unwanted software on infected systems.

Figure 1 — GPT-6 Astra campaign, attack chain.

GitHub Repositories

The initial access occurred via malicious GitHub repositories. The projects were impersonating ChatGPT and Claude related models, more specifically GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus. No manipulation of fake engagement (stars/forks) was in place.

Figure 2 — GitHub repository.

Aside from the repositories, GitHub.io pages were used to describe the capabilities of the software, while the malware was hosted as a release.

Figure 3 — GitHub.io page with links to malicious release.

These phishing landing pages contain download links that point directly to the malicious ZIP releases hosted on GitHub.

Figure 4 — Claude Opus GitHub[.]io page.

While the repositories do not show signs of fake engagement (such as artificially inflated stars or forks) that would promote them within GitHub’s own search, they still appear among the top results on Google. This is most likely due to SEO poisoning, where the attackers optimize titles, descriptions, and hosting domains to make their malicious projects rank highly in external search engines.

Figure 5 — Google Search results.

Each repository uses a different email address (edwardcarlsonmkym[@]outlook[.]com, daxschneiderdjuu[@]outlook[.]com, and rioprestonlfyx[@]outlook[.]com), and the uploader appears to operate in UTC+4, UTC-4, and UTC+3 respectively. This inconsistency likely reflects a deliberate attempt to obscure the threat actor’s true operational timezone.

Although the first repository was created around July 2026, the first two malicious releases were not uploaded until the end of August, and a third malicious release followed approximately five days later.

Release: /gpt-5-6/gpt-5-6.github.io/releases/tag/v5.6.0 [2026-08-30T19:15:44Z] gpt-5-6 Uploaded sol-setup.zip (application/zip) (269) ================================================== Release: /opus-5-0/opus-5-0.github.io/releases/tag/Release_v5.0.0 [2026-08-31T21:38:13Z] opus-5-0 uploaded Setup-Claude.zip (application/zip) (82) ================================================== Release: /gpt-6-astra/gpt-6-astra.github.io/releases/tag/Astra [2026-09-04T23:14:11Z] gpt-6-astra Uploaded GPT-6-Astra-Setup.zip (application/zip) (352)

Malicious zip files hosted on GitHub and other legitimate platforms are usually password-protected, since this prevents automated tools from unpacking and therefore analyzing them. However, neither of these repositories used password protection, as the binaries already had very low detection rates thanks to their anti-sandbox and other anti-analysis techniques.

Figure 6 — Low detection rate.

While the two ChatGPT-related releases and their repositories were created about five days apart, the ZIP files contain mostly the same files, including the malicious components, and they maintain the same IoCs.

The file that immediately stands out is winmm.dll, which was compiled the same day it was added to the ZIP archive. This suggests it is the component with the malicious functionality, while the other files serve to make the package appear legitimate. The compilation timestamp also indicates the actor is operating in the UTC-4 timezone.

Furthermore, Setup.exe, a legitimate signed OpenAI executable, is used during execution to sideload the malicious DLL. The Setup-Claude.zip file contains the same structure, though in this case Setup.exe is a legitimate signed Claude executable.

Figure 7 — Signed OpenAI and Anthropic binaries.

YobaDropper – winmm.dll

The malicious DLL contains multiple export names, suggesting that the legitimate winmm.dll has been spoofed. As in many other cases, these exports exist but their code has been stripped out, leaving them mostly empty and reducing the size of the binary.

Figure 8 — Stripped code from exports.

All 180 exports contain just a return instruction (C3) followed by NOPs (90), and DllEntryPoint is the only one containing actual code.

Anti-Analysis, Pre-Checks

The first function implements an anti-sandbox technique: the malware hashes the basename of its host executable and checks whether the checksum matches the hardcoded value 0xE6C2F326. The hashing algorithm has been identified as DJB2, which other malware families have also used in the past. The malware expects to run under the name Setup.exe, so this check fails if the DLL is executed on its own inside a sandbox environment.

Figure 9 — DJB2 algorithm and hash check.

Although a failed check does not terminate the process, the DLL performs 200,000 iterations of Sleep(5500), amounting to approximately 12.73 days, while repeatedly appending the decoded filler string pddy to a local UTF-16 buffer.

In the second function, the malware checks whether the infected user is located in a CIS country by inspecting the system’s keyboard layout. Ukraine was historically included in such checks, but it is not in the list used by recent malware.

The language check is unusual. Instead of comparing the victim’s keyboard language ID against hardcoded values, the malware checks whether the ID falls within the range 0x19–0x44. For IDs in that range, it tests the corresponding bit in the bitmask 0xEC0400C8401 to determine whether the language belongs to a CIS-region country, with an explicit exception for ID 0x22 (Ukrainian). Bazarloader has used a similar technique in the past, with the bitmask 0xD8080190C03.

Figure 10 — Language checks.

Language IDs excluded from the infection:

Russian

Belarusian

Tajik

Armenian

Azerbaijani

Georgian

Kazakh

Kyrgyz

Turkmen

Uzbek

Tatar

The malware continues to resolve Windows API functions dynamically from kernel32.dll and ntdll.dll by comparing hashes of the exported function names. The hashing algorithm is again DJB2, with the initial value 0x1505.

The last check before the malware unpacks and deploys the embedded payload tests whether the process is running with administrator privileges. If it is not, the malware displays the message “Please run this program as Administrator.” to the victim and terminates itself, requiring the user to rerun it with elevated privileges.

Deploying Phase

The dropper contains multiple XOR-encrypted strings that are decrypted when needed. These strings include the file paths where the embedded binaries are dropped, as well as the decryption keys.

It creates a directory under ProgramData named WMProcess. Then it copies the original WMPDMC.exe from System32 into this newly created folder. Next, it decrypts the embedded payload using the string IRANNUMBERONE as the XOR seed and drops the decrypted payload in the same folder under the name wmpdui.dll.

Using scheduled tasks, the dropper maintains persistence by leveraging the legitimate executable, which will sideload the malicious payload. To make the task appear legitimate, it sets the author to Microsoft Corporation and the description to Collects device metadata for Windows Media Player.. It also sets the boot-trigger delay to PT3M, which corresponds to a 3-minute delay after system startup, and configures the task to run under the Local System account (S-1-5-18).

YobaLoader – wmpdui.dll

The second-stage payload contains the same code as the dropper, which indicates that the same developer is responsible for both components.

The same anti-sandbox technique is used, forcing the malware to be run only by WMPDMC.exe. It again checks the hash of the process basename, and only continues execution if this value matches the hardcoded hash 0x552751E3.

The dropper uses the DJB2 hashing algorithm to hash and verify the process name and to resolve Windows API functions, both with the same seed 0x1505. The loader (YobaLoader) also uses DJB2 for the process name with the same seed as the dropper, but for resolving Windows API functions it uses a different seed, 0x1DEB.

Figure 11 — Hashing windows API functions.

The developer reused the same string-hashing algorithm but changed the seed (0x1505 in the dropper, 0x1DEB in the loader) to separate the hash spaces for each stage, complicating analysis, and reducing the effectiveness of hash-based detection and automated tooling.

Network

The downloader uses an interesting process to obtain the next-stage payload. It first decrypts multiple strings using a simple XOR operation, among these strings is the URL of a Telegram channel, t[.]me/yoba_fanclub. It then visits this channel using the user-agent string Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64;) and parses the HTML source to extract the src URL of the element with the class tgme_page_photo_image. This class refers to the location where the channel’s profile image is hosted.

Figure 12 — Telegram channel.

It downloads the image and uses the last 50 bytes as a seed to generate a domain based on three lists of dictionary words, which are decrypted as part of the DGA algorithm. This DGA algorithm uses three sets of strings:

Adjectives

Nouns

Verbs

Finally, it generates and appends an integer value in the range 0–999. The generated domain has the following format, "$adjective-$noun-$verb-$digit.dedyn[.]io". By changing the image of the Telegram channel, a new domain can be generated.

The following Python snippet represents the DGA algorithm:

""" Author: @Tera0017/Check Point Research """ from pathlib import Path import sys ADJECTIVES = [ "silver", "amber", "wild", "tiny", "brave", "lucky", "calm", "sharp", "swift", "bright", "quiet", "bold", "gentle", "fierce", "royal", "mystic", "username", "degenerate", "allblack", "kizta", "graf", ] NOUNS = [ "tiger", "river", "stone", "cloud", "wolf", "ocean", "forest", "mountain", "eagle", "raven", "ember", "comet", "fox", "dragon", "piano", "viper", "yoba", "yyoba", "static", "cpp", "example", ] VERBS = [ "runs", "jumps", "sings", "sleeps", "flies", "hunts", "burns", "floats", "shines", "whispers", "roars", "dreams", "strikes", "glides", "watches", "hides", "duty", "free", ] FNV_MULTIPLIER = 0x1000193 MASK64 = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF def hash_bytes(data: bytes, seed: int) -> int: value = seed for byte in data: value = ((value ^ byte) * FNV_MULTIPLIER) & MASK64 return value def generate_domain(image_path: str) -> str: image = Path(image_path).read_bytes() if len(image) < 50: raise ValueError("Image must contain at least 50 bytes") tail = image[-50:] adjective = ADJECTIVES[hash_bytes(tail, 0x811C9DC5) % len(ADJECTIVES)] noun = NOUNS[hash_bytes(tail, 0xAF0154A5) % len(NOUNS)] verb = VERBS[hash_bytes(tail, 0xFE5439E4) % len(VERBS)] number = hash_bytes(tail, 0xFFA7471A) % 1000 return f"{adjective}-{noun}-{verb}-{number}.dedyn[.]io" if __name__ == "__main__": image_file = sys.argv[1] print(generate_domain(image_file))

It then queries Google’s DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) API to obtain an encrypted command from a DNS TXT record, using a URL of the form https://dns[.]google/resolve?name=$DGA&type=TXT.

By relying on a DoH service and common file-hosting platforms, the actor aims to bypass passive DNS monitoring and some gateway-based security protections, making their command-and-control traffic harder to distinguish from regular user activity.

Figure 13 — DNS TXT record, base64 encoded data.

It decodes the Base64-encoded data field from the JSON response and validates it using Ed25519 signature verification with the public key b5c2d20623d4e6647d06a42864edd8629f82c5c384b243fdaeeeca24b3873d64. Once the signature validation succeeds, it decrypts the decoded value using AES in ECB mode with the key 1d0d1368b4d53f3a6322cf40e84e63db.

Decrypted response: 1https://files.catbox[.]moe/z5zpy9.dat

The downloader retrieves the encrypted payload and decrypts it using the same AES key and ECB mode that were previously used for the DNS data.

The malware provides three methods for deploying the downloaded payload. The selected method is indicated by the first character of the decrypted response that follows the URL (1/2/3):

Injects the downloaded payload into svchost.exe (NtWriteVirtualMemory/NtCreateThreadEx). It enumerates running processes and, using the hashing algorithm with the seed 0x1DEB, searches for the hash value 0xC26CDEA5, which corresponds to svchost.exe.

Saves the payload as a %TEMP%\$10_rand_char\$10_rand_char.exe file and executes it. Before running the executable, the downloader removes the Zone.Identifier alternate data stream, which is hidden metadata used by Windows to track the origin of downloaded files.

Saves the payload as a %TEMP%\$10_rand_char\$10_rand_char.ps1 PowerShell script and invokes it with the following parameters: -WindowStyle Hidden -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File.

Past Yoba Versions

Yoba exposes, through the same hashing algorithm it uses for anti-analysis, the specific process name under which it expects to run. Even without having full visibility into the campaign from the very beginning, analysts can still infer which targeted software was used to lure users by correlating this expected process name with the fake AI applications promoted on the associated GitHub repositories and GitHub Pages sites.

Earlier YobaDropper observed in the wild appeared in early June 2026. In this campaign, the dropper was sideloaded by a process named Cursor.exe (hash: 0x56221573). It remains unclear whether Cursor.exe was a legitimate signed binary. The majority of the functionality in this early variant is consistent with the newer versions of both the dropper and the loader.

YobaDropper shows two main differences between its older and newer versions:

Unpacking logic: In the oldest version, the buffer is first Base64-decoded and then XOR-decrypted to extract the YobaLoader. In the newer version, the developer removed the Base64-decoding step and performs only XOR decryption, simplifying the unpacking process.

Execution method: The second change concerns how YobaLoader is triggered. The newer version uses Scheduled Tasks to start the copied legitimate host and sideload the loader, whereas the first discovered version creates the shortcut msdefender_scheduler{7940-8490-6670-1081}.lnk in the Startup folder. This shortcut executes a copied %APPDATA%\Microsaft Difendir\msdtc.exe and sideloads %APPDATA%\Microsaft Difendir\mswsock.dll.

Earlier version of YobaLoader contains language checks and excludes only Russia from infection. In later versions, these checks were moved to the dropper stage and expanded to exclude additional CIS countries, shifting regional filtering earlier in the infection chain.

Figure 14 — Exclusion of Russian language from infection.

While the overall DGA logic remains the same, the early variant uses the extension .aber[.]ir instead of .dedyn[.]io. In addition, instead of injecting into svchost.exe, this variant injects into a different running process identified only by its hashed name 0x21BD94C2.

The initial loader also implements several anti-analysis techniques that have been removed from the newer versions of the malware:

1. Anti-debuggingIt enumerates all kernel object types and reads their TypeName values. Each type name is hashed using DJB2 with the seed 0x1DEB until the hash matches 0xCF9EE149, which corresponds to DebugObject. If a DebugObject is found, it indicates that a debugger is or was active, and in that case the malware terminates itself.

Figure 15 — DebugObject via NtQueryObject-ObjectAllTypesInformation.

2. Anti-VMThe malware uses a VM/sandbox-detection scoring function while running several hardware fingerprinting checks. The maximum score is 6, and the minimum required to continue the infection chain is 3. The checks include:

Hypervisor-present bit and CPUID timing (via RDTSCP).

Hypervisor vendor signature string (CPUID leaf 0x40000000).

CPU brand string sanity checks (CPUID leaves 0x80000002–0x80000004).

SMBIOS-based firmware fingerprinting (GetSystemFirmwareTable–RSMB)

Figure 16 — Hypervisor vendor signature string technique.

Despite these small differences in early anti-analysis behavior, the Telegram channel and the profile image used as the seed for the DGA remain the same as in the newer variants, indicating that the operator retained the same infrastructure while iterating on the loader’s evasion logic.

Conclusion

The Yoba campaign shows how attackers can use trusted platforms and the current interest in AI tools to distribute malware in a way that looks believable and harmless at first glance. By packaging their code together with well-known software names and hosting it on GitHub, they lower the chances that users or basic security checks will immediately flag the files as suspicious.Although the underlying techniques are more advanced than typical commodity malware, the main goals remain straightforward: gain a foothold on the victim’s system, avoid easy detection, and then run the attacker’s chosen payload. Organizations should be cautious about installing “AI helpers” or similar tools from unverified repositories and should enforce policies that restrict running software from unknown sources. Combining user awareness with basic technical controls.

Title: Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude
Context: Over the past several months, our scientists have engaged in deep research partnerships with six organizations developing new medicines: BigHat Biosciences, Bristol Myers...
Full Text:
Anthropic’s life sciences team is working to accelerate curing disease. Over the past several months, our scientists have engaged in deep research partnerships with six organizations developing new medicines: BigHat Biosciences, Bristol Myers Squibb, Divergence Labs, Enveda, Generate Biomedicines, and The Column Group. We've also begun drug discovery efforts of our own. In doing so, we've learned a lot about how Claude can support drug development, and how we’ll need to improve Claude further to realize AI's potential in medicine. We plan to scale this work up substantially from here.

There are many opportunities to speed up drug development, even beyond the most commonly discussed applications of AI, like proposing initial designs for new molecules. Developing a drug involves many varied tasks: doing early research to identify a target for a drug and the right type of drug to engage it, designing a molecule with the right properties, optimizing it to be manufactured reliably at scale, drafting the regulatory filings needed to run clinical trials, designing and administering those trials, and much more.

Our strategy to realize AI’s medical benefits is based on having AI increasingly involved in all of these tasks. There is no single problem to solve; the bottlenecks are distributed all throughout the drug development process. The best way to identify and work through these bottlenecks is to get deeply involved in real drug programs, across many different disease areas and stages of development.

So, over the past several months, we’ve partnered with six organizations to do so. We’ve also started drug discovery efforts of our own, including programs for rare childhood forms of muscular dystrophy, where Claude handles much of the scientific and operational work.

This work serves our goals in three ways. First, it lets us better understand the strengths and limitations of our models in relation to a much wider range of drug development tasks (we’ve already prioritized specific improvements to our models based on what we’ve learned so far). Second, these programs can serve as case studies for the wider life sciences community. If Claude is to significantly increase the rate of new cures, we need to work with many more biotechnology firms and integrate Claude more deeply into their development processes. Third, these projects should, if their positive trajectories continue, have direct impact themselves. We’re optimistic that some may result in effective new medicines for the diseases they target, including food allergies, rare childhood diseases, and several forms of cancer.

In this post, we provide an update on our progress with our partners, along with technical reports that describe our thought process, methods, and early results in more detail. We then briefly outline where our work is headed next.

Case studies

Generate Biomedicines: modality engineering. Generate Biomedicines has been working on increasing the usefulness of a cancer treatment known as CAR T-cell therapy. This therapy has historically helped treat blood cell cancers; Generate aims to reengineer it so that it can treat solid tumor cancers too. To do this, they’re aiming to shorten one part of the therapy’s genetic instructions, which would create room for additional instructions suited to other kinds of cancer. Six Generate scientists used Claude Code to propose new designs for this part. One design was about 70% shorter than the standard version, and in lab tests it was more effective: it allowed immune cells to make roughly 10 times as many receptors (the proteins they use to spot cancer cells), it killed tumor cells more efficiently, and the immune cells remained active for longer. Read more, and see Generate’s technical report.

Divergence Labs: hit generation. Divergence Labs is working on a novel way to treat food allergies. Food allergies are set off by a reaction from a molecule called IgE, some of which is attached to our immune cells and some of which floats freely in our blood. Divergence Labs is developing drugs that would detach the IgE from our immune cells entirely, rather than solely neutralizing the IgE circulating in our blood, as standard medications do. This could provide a much more effective treatment, but it requires a precise design, with two “arms”: one that would bind tightly to IgE, and another that would help prise IgE from the immune cell. Claude converted Divergence Labs’ goals into a detailed design plan, and then, largely autonomously, generated roughly 35,000 antibody designs in about a month to be narrowed down and tested. In those early tests, Divergence found “hits” for both arms: three designs that could bind to IgE, and 20 that could dislodge it. Three of those 20 appeared to dislodge IgE more than the standard medication. Its next step is to build a drug that combines the two arms. Read more, and see Divergence’s technical report.

BigHat Biosciences: lead optimization. BigHat Biosciences pairs AI with an automated lab to improve potential drugs (or “leads”), which must bind their target tightly, remain stable through manufacturing and storage, and avoid clumping together (among other criteria). BigHat’s scientists and an Anthropic researcher worked with Claude to improve these three properties in two leads, both antibody fragments that could become parts of future drugs: one designed to target cancer cells, and one designed to keep a drug in the body longer. Claude, connected to BigHat’s lab data system, Reccy, proposed changes to each molecule, and BigHat’s lab made and tested about 1,010 variants in about 10 weeks. Partway through, the team suspected the standard heat-stability and clumping metrics were misleading. Claude and the researcher reanalyzed the raw data, then proposed different metrics and a protocol change to test them. BigHat’s scientists refined and ran it, and the main predictions held. Compared with the originals, the best versions bound more than 10x more tightly, the cancer-targeting lead stayed in solution 18°C higher, and the lead for longer-lasting drugs clumped more than 100x more slowly. Read more, and see BigHat’s technical report.

Enveda: manufacturing and filings. To conduct clinical trials, companies need records showing that each batch of a new drug has been made to strict quality standards, and to submit an application to regulators, among other requirements. At Enveda, manufacturing chemists spent up to 75% of their time on paperwork. To ease the load, Enveda built a system that connects all of its manufacturing documents to Claude, then lets Claude flag any possible issues. Over tests on 1,061 pages of documentation, Claude caught all 11 issues that human reviewers had spotted—and flagged seven they’d missed. In the process, this method reduced human review time by 89%, from over 25 hours to less than three. Separately, Claude wrote the first drafts of two important regulatory documents. One took four hours, compared to about three months by hand. For the other, Enveda’s standard human review process found one minor error. Read more, and see Enveda’s technical report.

The Column Group (TCG): company creation. Because drug discovery can be slow, expensive, and prone to failure, investors in biotechnology companies have favored safer, previously validated ideas over riskier new ones, even when the latter could help more patients. We’ve been working with TCG to see whether Claude can change this by cutting the time and cost of drug discovery so that investors can confidently support more ambitious ideas. Specifically, TCG is establishing Pleiades, a new company that will use Claude to run many more—and more complex—drug programs than is usual for a small team. This could be a model for how Claude can reduce both the scientific and the operational and administrative overhead required to run a biotechnology company. If this works, this model could be replicated across the industry and direct investment toward harder problems in medicine. Pleiades is currently developing new tools and workflows for Claude; its very first Claude skill, which helps Claude assess whether drug targets are worth pursuing, has been evaluated on 45 target-disease pairs. Read more.

More recently, we’ve also begun working with Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) to find and address bottlenecks in clinical trial planning. BMS is using Claude to assess plans of an early-stage drug in clinical trials, and to estimate the likelihood of those trials succeeding. Together, we plan to expand this work in 2027 to understand its potential for increasing the probability of success in early development.

“We use Claude at the clinical trial stage to analyze proprietary data, create a clinical study plan, and weigh the study’s chance of success. From a single prompt, Claude generated a robust initial analysis that helped inform our assessment of different development options, which would otherwise take days to complete. We did all of this while ensuring the security of our highly sensitive data. We look forward to expanding this work across our pipeline to support portfolio-level decisions.”

Michael Pourdehnad, MD, Senior Vice President, Head of Early Clinical Development, Hematology, Oncology and Cell Therapy.

In addition to our work with these partners, we’ve begun to run some research programs ourselves. We’ve acquired Mithril Medicine, a one-person company that has been developing treatments for two rare forms of muscular dystrophy. Its founder, Cody Tranbarger, used Claude to organize contracts, logistics, and experiments with 11 external labs, and delegated many other aspects of Mithril’s operations to Claude. As a result, Mithril took a possible treatment for one form of muscular dystrophy from an idea to promising results in mice in less than 18 months. Now at Anthropic, Cody is continuing this research, and plans to start several new programs. If his drug candidates continue to hold up, we expect a drug to be ready to start clinical trials in humans as soon as late 2028. Read more and see our technical report.

Extending our work in the life sciences

All of this research is still at an early stage. In particular, so far it is mostly preclinical—that is, for the most part, it isn’t yet at the stage where the drugs are being tested in humans. We plan to continue extending Claude’s role into clinical trials as these drug programs advance, and as we partner with more organizations whose drug development programs are already at the clinical stage.

This research is only one part of our efforts to accelerate drug discovery. Ultimately, we want to share our models with as many drug development researchers as possible. To that end, we’ve rolled out Claude Science, our AI workbench for researchers, and we’re providing Claude credits for life scientists. We’ve also created the Life Sciences Verification Program to allow trusted organizations to use our most powerful models with more permissive versions of our safeguards, which are necessary to prevent misuse but which can impede legitimate biological research. We’ve also recently launched an open call for guest investigators in the life sciences; we’re seeking proposals from research groups who want to use Claude to investigate key questions in drug discovery and other areas.

We’re looking forward to working with many more organizations as we expand our life sciences research. If you work at an organization focused on drug discovery and are interested in collaborating with us, you can get in touch below.

Title: Expanding our partnership with GSA to bring Claude to all levels of government

We are expanding our partnership with the General Services Administration (GSA) through a new agreement that gives government partners a 40% discount on Claude Enterprise, Claude for Government, and the Claude API. For the first time, the discount applies across every product surface, including when agencies buy from us directly today and through cloud providers in the coming months. The discount also extends to state, local, tribal and territorial governments.

We are also launching a dedicated program to help agencies implement and make the most of their Claude use. These programs are commonly leveraged by our private sector customers and we’re looking forward to bringing those best practices to our public sector partners in the coming weeks.

Approximately 500 US federal, state, and local government organizations now use Claude. Weekly Claude for Government active users are up about eightfold since February, and usage across federal civilian agencies has grown about 20-fold in a year. Those organizations run some of the most important systems in the country, usually on tight budgets and with long procurement cycles. This agreement is built to support that work, so they can apply Claude to hard problems without a large upfront commitment.

The discounts offered through the agreement are estimated to save the government $1 billion. Agencies are not bound by a minimum spend commitment and will be able to pay for the usage they consume.

How Claude is helping public servants get more done

Government agencies are using Claude to solve some of their most important challenges. Examples include managing backlogs, records and forms, and modernizing old code. Some of the ways agencies are using Claude include:

Utah gave Claude Code to 34 developers across 10 state agencies. 80% had a working environment within 30 minutes, 71% reported saving 20+ hours by the end of the four-week pilot.

A US state CIO confirmed their team was able to respond to a ransomware attack in 8 minutes vs. the usual 2-3 days thanks to Claude.

A US federal security team used Claude Mythos to detect and patch the vulnerability that would have allowed for the takeover of a critical production system in about two days. A human penetration test the month before had missed it.

A cybersecurity professional at a major agency found and patched bugs in critical financial systems.

A US state IT developer moved nearly 900 API methods to a new framework in two days. The project had been scoped for a month.

A US state IT director used Claude Code to document 12 legacy code repositories, mapping 467 database tables and flagging 27 risks along the way.

More than half of the US states, some of the largest localities, and some of the countries largest critical infrastructure operators participated in our SLTT cyber defense program.

Meeting government security requirements

Agencies can use Claude for their most sensitive unclassified work. Claude for Government, which delivers Claude's coding and agentic work capabilities and provides near-feature parity with commercial offerings at a FedRAMP High authorization level, was made generally available on September 30.

Agencies building their own tools can use Claude through Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud’s Vertex AI. On Bedrock, Claude is authorized for FedRAMP High, with select models authorized for DoD IL4 and IL5 workloads in AWS GovCloud. On Vertex AI, Claude is authorized for FedRAMP High.

Claude Enterprise is in process for FedRAMP Moderate authorization through the FedRAMP 20x program, marking the next evolution of how we are bringing the same innovative technology available commercially to the government.

Getting started

Government agencies can buy Claude at the OneGov discount through GSA's Multiple Award Schedule today. Whether your department or agency already uses Claude or is interested in using it, our Public Sector team will help discuss your options.

Title: Manage costs and demonstrate ROI for Claude Code on Google Cloud
Context: Combine these capabilities to control your overall bill, but remember that control is only the first lever
Full Text:
As organizations delegate more work to Claude Code, spend grows with it, and platform teams need a way to both control costs and understand impact. Inspired by a recent webinar (opens in new tab) with Google Cloud, we share how organizations using Claude Code can better track and optimize these considerations on Google Cloud, including three core levers: control, track, and prove.

Controls for managing Claude Code spend

Claude on Google Cloud has consumption-based pricing, so your bill is a readout of how much your developers are using Claude in your Google Cloud environment. Adoption drives usage; usage is what you pay for, and it’s also where the value shows up.

Your Claude Code bill is a product of how many tokens tasks consume and the models that handle them. Token consumption scales with task complexity and conversation length. Chat is a Q&A conversation. An agentic tool like Claude Code spends more tokens per task relative to chat because it's doing multistep work: reading files, running tools, and reasoning across a whole task. Meanwhile each model has its own price per token, so matching the model to the task is the other major cost control.

Visibility into the tokens and model choices impacting your organization’s bill each month is available through the Claude apps gateway and Google Cloud services. You can govern the spend and manage costs via three independent levers:

Control. Creating guardrails that guide usage without over-restricting access and unintentionally blocking people.

Track. Granular oversight of where the spend is happening, and where it will continue to go, before the bill arrives.

Prove. Identifying the value your org is getting from spending these tokens and attributing exactly where it’s coming from.

Here’s how to apply this control -> track -> prove framework to your own Claude Code on Google Cloud deployment.

The governance toolbox

Claude on Google Cloud comes with tools and capabilities for controlling, tracking, and proving the value of your spend.

Google Cloud already gives you many native capabilities you can apply to tracking and controlling your Claude spend:

Per-project billing. Allows you to host a dedicated project for Claude Code as a clean way to track costs.

Billing budgets and alerts. Allows you to set budget alerts and get notified as actual spend crosses thresholds you define.

Spend caps (Preview). Allows you to enforce a service-level Google Cloud spend budget with ability to manually lift the cap.

BigQuery exports. Lets you analyze Claude spend alongside the rest of your cloud costs.

Quotas. Claude models on Google Cloud have per-minute limits on requests, input tokens, and output tokens for each model family and endpoint location.

Provisioned throughput. Pay a fixed fee for reserved capacity instead of pay-as-you-go.

Claude Code and Claude apps gateway add their own tracking and control capabilities. The gateway is a self-hosted service, shipped in the same claude binary your developers already use, that runs in your Google Cloud project between Claude Code and Claude on Google Cloud. Developers sign in through your identity provider, such as Google Workspace, so every request carries a verified identity. That lets you set model allowlists per IdP group, and spend caps per user, IdP group, or organization, by day, week, or month.

Here's how to choose and combine capabilities to manage the three levers measuring the cost and ROI behind your organization’s AI investments with Claude on Google Cloud:

Lever 1: Control

The control lever is all about providing guardrails that guide developers in their Claude Code use, instead of restricting them with arbitrary caps.

Guiding rather than restricting is important because high cost sessions are not necessarily bad — in fact, they're often high value, especially in Claude Code. Those sessions are generally your power users that are at the forefront, using new workflows and getting a lot of value from Claude and getting a lot of work done.

Waste tends to sit in the long middle of heavy spenders. For example, they're using Fable for a daily routine that Sonnet can easily handle. Or maybe they have forgotten some scheduled task they no longer care about, but it keeps on running automatically anyway.

There are four features that give you the guardrails to guide your users instead of restricting them:

Spend limits (opens in new tab). The Claude apps gateway allows you to set spend caps per user, per IdP group, or organization-wide, by day, week, or month. Group and organization caps are per-developer defaults that each member inherits, not a shared pool.

Threshold alerts. When used with Claude apps gateway, Claude Code on Google Cloud warns developers as they approach their cap, first past 75% and again past 95%. These are in-CLI warnings for developers, whereas Google Cloud Billing alerts are meant for admins. At the cap, the gateway returns 429 until the period resets or an admin raises the cap, and you can script cap increases through the gateway's admin API.

Model defaults and allowlists. Specify which models are available, per IdP group, via the Claude apps gateway which enforces the allowlist server-side on every request. We have found that setting a model default works really well, because most people will stick to the model default; if they want to switch models, they usually are switching for a reason. You can use model defaults in addition to or instead of model allowlists.

Gateway Admin API. The gateway serves an admin API for spend limits (opens in new tab), so you can set and change caps programmatically, for example using a ticketing workflow.

Combine these capabilities to control your overall bill, but remember that control is only the first lever. Price per token doesn't give you the full picture. The most important metric is the cost per task, which can be monitored and analyzed by tracking this usage.

Lever 2: Track

This lever is all about seeing where spend is going and how it’s being used. The good news is that you can track Claude Code usage, costs, and tool activity across your organization. Primary tracking strategies include:

Usage and cost observability. Claude Code's OpenTelemetry metrics and events (opens in new tab) report usage and estimated cost, broken down by skill, plugin, agent, and MCP server. Send them over OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) to tools you already run, such as Google Cloud Monitoring, through an OpenTelemetry collector or relayed by the Claude apps gateway (for centralized OpenTelemetry config).

End-user usage view. Developers see their own spend and get usage warnings right in Claude Code before they hit a limit.

Data export to your existing systems. Google Cloud Billing exports to BigQuery let you filter to Claude SKUs by model and token type, putting Claude spend alongside the rest of your cloud and AI spend. OTel flows to your O11y stack, and the gateway Admin API can feed spend-limit status straight into your ticketing system.

Lever 3: Prove

The control lever governs and apportions usage and costs; the track lever allows you to visualize that spend. The prove lever is how you map usage to ROI for Claude Code on Google Cloud.

The metrics that platform engineers care most about measuring in Claude Code are contained within three dimensions: usage, developer satisfaction, and impact.

Adoption and usage metrics measure how people are using Claude in your organization, including your activated users and their weekly and daily usage. These reveal information like depth of use, user retention over time, and who your Claude Code power users are. These metrics are all derived via Claude Code OTel data.

Satisfaction metrics monitor the user experience for your engineers, including their happiness with Claude Code, perceived time savings, confidence in output, and any friction they might experience. Satisfaction metrics come from a short survey run before and after rollout, followed by ongoing user check-ins.

Impact metrics assess how Claude is delivering measurable engineering outcomes, comparing throughput, cycle time, and review speed against a baseline, plus qualitative measurements on specific bodies of work.

A starting set of impact metrics

Here's a starting set of impact metrics, grouped into three areas: time, effort, and volume.

Time measures how quickly work ships: PR cycle time from open -> merge, and code review turnaround.

Effort measures how much work each change takes: review iterations per PR, review comments and rework per PR.

Volume measures what the freed-up capacity delivers: PRs per engineer, deployment frequency, and named bodies of work: the specific backlog items your teams shipped with the freed capacity. These add a qualitative view alongside the counts..

These are directional reference points, not rules, but a good starting point for measuring Claude Code's impact in your organization. The baseline you need already exists: your delivery history in source control and tickets.

Define your unit of work

Most of these metrics count PRs, but a typo fix and a feature release are both one PR. Therefore, count merged PRs of a defined class instead: Claude opens the PR, and a person decides whether it ships. Labels such as hotfix or feature release, the ticket ID, and whether Claude was involved make those PRs easy to find in the systems you already run. Not every unit of work is a PR; a service cutover or an incident closed at its root cause are examples. The same rule applies: count one finished thing, where it lands.

Logging user prompts, for example, is a good way to understand everything your user base is trying to build, because not every unit of work is necessarily a PR. Note that user prompts are not logged automatically due to potentially sensitive content; you have to specifically opt in.

One example would be using Claude Code to troubleshoot an incident if you’re an SRE or generate sample data for a live demo if you’re a sales engineer. Those sessions do not result in a PR, but they do accelerate those teams’ workflows. Keep in mind that Claude Code's PR metric counts the PRs Claude Code creates, not what eventually merges.
