Title: Discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities in critical, real-world software with Claude
Context: Finally, Claude discovered a use-after-free in FedCM, Chrome’s federated sign-in feature, that allowed the exploit to execute arbitrary code outside the sandbox
Full Text:
Over the past few months, we’ve used an unreleased, internal research model to find critical vulnerabilities in some of the world’s most widely used software, such as browsers and operating systems. In this post, we share details of five attack chains, which led to remote code execution and other critical impacts with little to no user interaction. These attack chains demonstrate the model’s ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software. Any vulnerabilities in these products could affect billions of users. They’re also among the most security-critical software in the world, making them a bellwether for testing models’ vulnerability research and cyber capabilities.

We reported each vulnerability to the affected vendor under our coordinated vulnerability disclosure, which gives developers 90 days to patch and a further 45 days before we discuss details beyond what is already included in a public advisory.

1. One-click remote code execution in Chrome

After initial prompting, Claude wrote a full exploit chain enabling an attacker to execute arbitrary code as the user, outside the browser’s sandbox. Our proof of concept launches the Calculator app from a stock default-configuration Chrome browser on macOS within seconds of the page loading, without any further user interaction:

Claude discovered a vulnerability in Chrome’s JavaScript engine, V8, that allowed a malicious web page to corrupt V8’s heap memory.

Claude discovered a second vulnerability to break out of V8’s memory region sandbox and defeat ASLR. This step located Chrome’s code in memory and used a return-oriented programming (ROP) chain to take full control of the renderer process.

The compromised renderer was confined by Chrome’s process sandbox. Claude then discovered a race condition in CacheStorage. The compromised renderer used the race condition to read memory outside the sandbox and learn the memory layout of the privileged browser process.

Finally, Claude discovered a use-after-free in FedCM, Chrome’s federated sign-in feature, that allowed the exploit to execute arbitrary code outside the sandbox.

We have reported our findings to Google: 62 CVEs have been assigned and patched as of Chrome 156, with all of them rated critical or high severity. Among them are 13 sandbox escapes and 21 vulnerabilities that could have been used to compromise the renderer.

2. A one-click exploit chain in Safari

After initial prompting, Claude wrote an exploit chain that let any website’s JavaScript completely bypass the same-origin policy (SOP). The exploit could access a user’s Safari history, cookies, and other sensitive data, and could send authenticated HTTP requests to other domains and read the responses. For example, if the user is signed in to their email account, the attacker can now read their email; if they’re logged into their bank account, the attacker can view account balances or attempt transfers.

To do this, Claude defeated several layers of protection built into Safari:

Claude discovered a use-after-free (UAF) vulnerability in JavaScriptCore, Safari’s JavaScript engine, which is written in C++. Certain TypedArray operations wrote through stale pointers to freed memory, overwriting TypedArray metadata.

WebKit’s Gigacage mitigates this type of attack by isolating TypedArray data in a separate region of memory. Claude discovered that certain variables in this region were used to index into other regions, which gave it an arbitrary read/write primitive outside the Gigacage.

All website JavaScript runs in the WebContent sandbox, which keeps bugs like the UAF from reaching sensitive browser data on disk. Claude discovered a vulnerability in the sandbox's IPC mechanism that let the exploit read Safari’s stored history, cookies, and session databases from disk.

Finally, Claude used the UAF to overwrite a variable in memory and disable the SOP, allowing the attacker’s page to read data from any other origin.

The chain is interesting because it is a data-only attack that never relies on arbitrary code execution. Instead, it uses full read/write access to the browser process’s memory to modify a security flag, an object size, and a URL. Several of the weaknesses are not vulnerabilities on their own but intended behaviors that become exploitable when combined.

Apple acknowledged our report the same day we submitted it and implemented a fix promptly. That fix is available to users.

3. Android lock screen bypass

After initial prompting, Claude wrote an exploit that let an attacker extract photos and other personal information from a stolen Android phone without unlocking it. The work combined three methods: source code analysis of the open-source parts of Android, reverse engineering and deobfuscation of the Google Play services binaries, and live testing on a physical Google Pixel 9. This turned up a wide range of vulnerabilities in both the open-source and proprietary components. Claude then chained three of them into the final exploit.

Android has several layers of protection against this attack. Claude found a way around each one:

A locked Android phone is designed not to transfer data over USB. Claude found that a USB host with a specific setting bypassed this.

The device-to-device transfer protocol refuses data commands from unauthorized peers. Claude found a way to skip the authorization check and start the pairing process.

Pairing is protected by an authenticated key agreement that asks the user to verify a six-digit code. Claude found a flaw that skipped this verification and behaved as if the user had tapped “Allow.”

USB transfers are not supposed to carry file contents, as enforced by a hardcoded check. Claude found a fallback mechanism that sent raw bytes over USB and was not covered by the check. The exploit requested file contents through it.

This issue has been addressed by Google.

4. Windows remote denial of service

After initial prompting, Claude wrote an exploit that would have allowed an attacker to remotely crash any Windows machine that responds to HTTP/3 requests using the native Windows implementation. The difficulty in this case was in identifying the vulnerability in the first place. Following that initial prompting, we reported this vulnerability directly to Microsoft, which resolved the vulnerability and assigned it CVE-2026-33096.

The vulnerability that Claude identified was a memory safety out-of-bounds read in the Windows kernel’s implementation of QUIC. An attacker could reach the vulnerable codepath remotely over the network and send a few packets of data to a listening server to crash and restart the machine. By repeatedly sending these requests, it is possible to continuously crash the server, which causes loss of access to the server for all of the users. We estimate that there are likely several million such servers listening on the internet.

Claude discovered this vulnerability through binary analysis. We provided the model with a copy of the Windows executable and asked Claude to reverse-engineer how the software works using the existing reverse-engineering tools (such as Ghidra), write a fully annotated C program that reproduces the relevant features, compare the behavior reproduced program to binary to ensure correctness, and then study the code for vulnerabilities. When we asked Claude to identify potentially higher-risk issues, it surfaced this remotely exploitable vulnerability.

5. Zero-click remote code execution in Linux

While this post focuses on third-party products, our work on open source has continued. With Claude, we discovered local privilege escalation vulnerabilities on OpenBSD, FreeBSD, and Linux; a number of sandbox escapes in popular sandboxing infrastructure; and numerous vulnerabilities in important web applications. We have also found remotely triggerable (zero-click) arbitrary code execution vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel’s networking stack, which have since been patched upstream and publicly disclosed. We detail one such example below.

After initial prompting, Claude wrote an exploit that allows a remote attacker to send packets to Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener to run arbitrary commands as root, without any credentials or user interaction. The underlying vulnerability is a race condition-induced UAF bug in the kernel networking stack. The full exploitation has two key stages:

In the first stage, the attacker defeats KASLR remotely. It exploits the race to make the kernel read an attacker-controlled length field to copy extra bytes and send them back to the attacker, and as long as one such overread contains a kernel pointer in the reply, the attacker learns the kernel address space layout.

In the second stage, the attacker hijacks the control flow. It exploits the same UAF bug to overflow a buffer and overwrite a callback pointer with the address of a payload the attacker has already staged in kernel memory via an ordinary protocol feature. When the kernel invokes the callback, the payload chains a series of calls to existing kernel functions. ending with an attacker-chosen shell command running as root.

An enabling property of this race condition is that a lost race only fails the handshake without crashing the whole system, so a determined attacker can retry indefinitely until they succeed. In our proof of concept, it takes 48 minutes to leak a kernel pointer and another five minutes to reach the shell command execution. This vulnerability (CVE-2026-98432) was patched upstream and backported to all maintained stable kernel branches.

What we learned

Throughout our process of using Claude for this security work, we identified a number of insights that shaped our approach. We think two are particularly important.

Test-time compute scaling and scanner diversity substantially increase how many vulnerabilities you find. We built a platform that runs large numbers of scanning agents in parallel, measures each scanner by how many additional vulnerabilities it contributes to the mix, and tracks coverage dynamically so the scanners process the entire codebase.

The strategies range from pure coverage (is there a vulnerability in this function?) to goal-based (does this app expose anything that could compromise customer data?) to threat model-based (does anything in this app bypass its documented threat model?). We also used Claude to run automated variant analysis on every confirmed finding. All findings pass through a standardized verification and risk rating pipeline, so we can experiment freely with new scanners without lowering the quality bar.

Fixing the existing backlog only solves half the problem; the other half is cutting the rate at which new vulnerabilities enter the codebase. For that, we recommend scanning at PR time. We built security guidance directly into our development process through a Claude Code plugin, which we’ve released publicly.

What this means for defenders

Frontier models have the ability to discover and combine multiple vulnerabilities into a working exploit. These skills have historically been the domain of few specialist teams with expertise in these targets. Now, it’s something models can do with little human involvement, and then prove by producing a working exploit that anyone can run and verify.

Enabling defenders with powerful models is critical to giving them a headstart on patching systems before attackers do. Recently, we released an expanded version of our Cyber Verification Program, which makes advanced cyber capabilities and reduced blocking classifiers available to qualifying security professionals. It includes access to our most capable models, including Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Mythos 5.1, and other new models moving forward. Our advice to defenders remains the same: scanning your own code is more important than ever.

Title: Mythos access is expanding: what this means for vulnerability management
Context: Product Marketing Manager @ linkedin Subscribe to Threat Research REGISTER FOR THE WEBINAR Published: October 27, 2026 Table of contents TRT in your inbox Get security briefings...
Full Text:
Anthropic’s Claude Mythos put vulnerability management in the boardroom when it was released earlier this year, and the conversation around it has evolved. Press coverage continues to find new angles, and there’s plenty of discourse around how AI is changing everything about cybersecurity.

In the months since the initial release of Mythos Preview, there have been a few developments around what Mythos can do and who is able to access it. But what does this actually mean for your vulnerability management program?

A stronger model, wider access

In September, Anthropic shipped Claude Mythos 5.1, which it calls the model with the strongest cyber capabilities of any they’ve released. Mythos 5.1 is built on the same base model as the generally available Fable 5.1 with different safeguards attached. Then, in October, it folded Project Glasswing, the early-access program that gave select critical infrastructure providers and industry partners access to Mythos, into an expanded tiered Cyber Verification Program (CVP). The revamped CVP spans everyday defensive work up through the highest-sensitivity critical infrastructure.

This means that compared to at launch, machine-speed vulnerability discovery that used to be limited to a small group will reach a wider set of defenders. According to Anthropic, Glasswing partners turned up more than 129,000 verified vulnerabilities between April and July, over 33,000 of them critical or high severity. More access to Mythos-class discovery sounds like it should mean more vulnerabilities found, faster, across more organizations. While this is true, that large number isn’t the full story.

Discovery and exploitation aren’t the same thing

Anthropic noted in its announcement that the generally available Fable 5.1 can now be used to discover software vulnerabilities, but explicitly not to develop exploits for them. Activities that could be used maliciously like penetration testing, exploit generation, etc., are redirected to lower-tier models. The same gating carries into Mythos. The CVP’s three access tiers wall off penetration testing and red teaming work behind the two highest, most heavily vetted tiers.

So while broader access to Mythos-class capability means broader access to finding things faster, it doesn’t, by itself, mean broader access to attacking anything. Also, Mythos still isn’t broadly available: access runs through vetted organizations in the CVP, so it isn’t something readily on hand for attackers.

That’s not to say automated attacks aren’t happening, but that’s a separate development, not something that traces back to Mythos specifically. Lumping every agentic AI risk together misses where the actual exposure is coming from.

The core of vulnerability management hasn’t changed

A lot of the coverage of Mythos makes it sound scarier than it needs to. While it does make vulnerability discovery significantly faster, no security team was patching every known CVE even before Mythos existed. Using AI agents for defense can increase teams’ speed and scope, but the real differentiator continues to be knowing which findings are in active, loaded packages, reachable, and creating real risk, versus which ones are noise with a scary CVSS score attached.

Exploits are getting faster too. Mandiant now puts the average time-to-exploit at negative seven days, meaning exploitation begins before a vulnerability is even disclosed. This makes it even more important to build a vulnerability management program around core principles.

The fundamentals of vulnerability management are even more important in the AI discovery era:

Scan and discover everything in one place, CVE and non-CVE findings alike.

Prioritize by what’s in-use and exploitable, not just what scores high.

Automate remediation at the source instead of patching every downstream instance individually.

Treat runtime security as a safety net for whatever stays exposed.

This plan for vulnerability response doesn’t get rewritten because discovery got faster. Agentic AI can be utilized on your side too, automating and accelerating each of these steps and helping keep up with the volume of findings. You don’t need to treat every Mythos headline as a crisis or rebuild your program every time access expands again.

Learn more at the webinar

To learn more about building a Mythos-ready vulnerability management program, join our webinar, Mythos Decoded: What’s Actually Changed in Vulnerability Management. We’ll cover what Mythos actually is and isn’t and practical steps to keep pace with AI-accelerated discovery without the panic.

More than 25,000 nonprofits now use Claude in their work. Most of those organizations are small, local operations: more than 75% of them have fewer than 10 Claude seats. We think today's update will have the biggest impact on these organizations.

We’ve spent the last year working directly with nonprofits to meet their needs. We expanded nonprofit plans to the same models as our standard Team and Enterprise plans, lowered the Team plan minimum to orgs with as few as two people, and included Claude Code in nonprofit plans at no additional cost. And during the United Nations General Assembly in September, we launched a new discount of ~90% for verified nonprofits in low- and middle-income countries, bringing standard Team seats to $3/user/month.

Cost is only one barrier. Nonprofits told us two others stood in the way: a lack of people with the skills to put AI to work, and a lack of tools built specifically for how nonprofits operate.

Too few people with AI skills. Claude Corps is placing 1,000 early-career fellows in at least 400 US nonprofits to build with Claude alongside their teams. Hosts include a wide variety of organizations, from large organizations to small, local teams, including food banks, art museums, and veteran support organizations. We’re now planning to extend this program through a partnership with Taproot, which would match nonprofits with experienced pro bono consultants for shorter, project-based work. A growing group of partners can support nonprofit adoption, including Accenture, Boston Consulting Group (BCG), The Bridgespan Group, Civis Analytics, Deloitte, fusionSpan, Idealist Consulting, Myridius, SapienAI, Slalom, v4c.ai, and Vera Solutions. And for teams getting started on their own, we’re hosting two live webinars: Claude for Nonprofits: An Admin's Guide to Data Handling and AI Use Policy (opens in new tab), for admins, on November 10, and Claude for Nonprofits: A Staff Guide to Making Claude Useful on Day One (opens in new tab) on November 12.

Too few tools built to meet nonprofits where they’re at. We built the skills we're releasing today with the nonprofits in our Design Partner Circle. It includes ~30 organizations, from small teams serving one region of the United States to international organizations operating in dozens of countries, working on education, economic mobility, health, humanitarian response, and more. Many are funders themselves. This fall, fundraisers, operations leads, and chiefs of staff at many of these organizations tried early versions of our skills on real work and told us what wasn't working. We brainstormed, iterated, and updated our solution based on what we heard.

What's in the plugin

We’re starting with three areas nonprofits told us were most urgent, especially as year-end fundraising picks up.

Extend your team

Many nonprofits told us the same thing: there are more jobs to do than people to do them, so everyone covers several roles at once. Claude extends your team, so a small staff can work like a bigger one and spend more of its time on the mission.

Marketing: plan a campaign sized to your team’s bandwidth, teach Claude to draft in your organization’s voice, and get a second read on your content before it goes out.

Hiring and people: build a job post with an interview guide and scoring rubric, plan a new hire's first 90 days, and answer staff questions from your own handbook.

Board and leadership: see what skills your board is missing, draft outreach to the candidates you have in mind, get new members up to speed with an orientation packet, and plan the deck for your next meeting.

Set up Claude responsibly: security, governance, and context

Claude works best when it has your organization’s context, including your mission, programs, workstreams, communication principles, and policies, and when your staff have clear rules for working with it. Start by asking Claude to:

Map your organization. Claude asks where you keep each kind of record, like donor data, grant files, finances and policies, and, with memory on, saves that map for each person. It then offers to connect the tools it can't reach yet. Every other skill in the plugin reads the map first, so Claude knows where to look and you don't have to point it to the same source for each task.

Check what your AI policy allows. Staff can ask "Can I use Claude for this?" and get the answer based on your organization's own AI policy. (No policy yet? See the Claude Academy tutorial below.)

Fund your mission

Fundraising is the lifeline for nonprofits, and it matters even more toward the end of the year. It's also time-intensive and process-heavy, which can be challenging for small organizations. The plugin supports the full fundraising lifecycle, freeing up your team's time for the irreplaceable human work, like managing relationships and deciding which opportunities to pursue.

Find the right funders and grants. Research donors, foundations, companies, and surface open grants, with sources cited.

Decide what to pursue. Forward an RFP and get a breakdown on eligibility, requirements, and what it would take to compete.

Write proposals and reports. Turn an RFP into a requirements list and a first draft built from your own material. Grant reports include sources for their figures.

Keep relationships warm. Get a brief before a funder call, a write-up and thank-you note after, and donor updates in your voice. Ask how to re-engage donors and receive a stewardship plan.

Title: Physicist Christopher Stubbs joins Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust
Context: In 1998, as a member of the High-Z Supernova Search Team, he helped discover the accelerating expansion of the universe, work that later earned the team the Breakthrough Prize...
Full Text:
Dr. Christopher Stubbs, an experimental physicist and former Dean of Science at Harvard University, has joined Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust. He brings to the Trust decades of scientific expertise across observational cosmology and precision measurement. He has also advised the US government on national security and arms control.

“I am honored to join Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust and to help the company deliver on its public benefit mission,” said Stubbs. “I use AI tools in my research every day and see what they make possible, and as an educator I have confronted some of the hard questions they raise. As a grandfather, I want to help ensure that AI is developed and deployed for the long-term benefit of humanity.”

Stubbs is the Samuel C. Moncher Professor of Physics and of Astronomy at Harvard, where he served as Dean of Science from 2018 to 2024. In 1998, as a member of the High-Z Supernova Search Team, he helped discover the accelerating expansion of the universe, work that later earned the team the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics. He was also the inaugural project scientist for what is now the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which started a 10-year survey of the southern sky in June. One of its aims is to study the accelerating expansion he helped discover.

More recently, he’s written about how to keep AI-assisted research reproducible when models can give different answers to the same question. He’s a member of JASON, an independent group of scientists who have advised the US government on defense and technology since 1960.

“When Chris found evidence that the universe was expanding at a rate no one expected, he and his team followed the data even when it went against the prevailing wisdom of the field. As AI starts to transform how science itself is done, Chris’s intellectual honesty, rigor, and commitment to the truth are the values we want shaping the future of this technology, and I’m grateful he’s bringing his deep expertise to the Trust,” said Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President of Anthropic.

Anthropic is a Public Benefit Corporation, which means we’re structured to balance commercial growth with our public benefit purpose. The Trust exists to help us hold that balance over the long term. It has the authority to appoint a majority of Anthropic’s board, and Trustees advise the board and our leadership on critical decisions, particularly those involving risks and societal impacts of AI.

This week we published our first Public Benefit Report, a public account of how we’re working toward our charter and where we’re falling short. The Trustees helped define the five charter pillars it measures us against, and the report closes with their assessment of our progress to date. Subject to stockholder approval, we’ve also committed to setting aside a portion of Anthropic’s shares to Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows.

“Helping the world build powerful AI safely and making sure it meaningfully improves people’s lives both depend on a deep understanding of science and on leading with integrity,” added Neil Buddy Shah, Chair of the Long-Term Benefit Trust. “Not only has Chris worked on some of the hardest problems in science, but he has consistently been a high-integrity leader of large, complex, collaborative scientific endeavors across academia, government, and the national laboratories. That will be of great value to the Trust as we support Anthropic in developing AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.”

Stubbs, the Trust’s first physicist, joins Shah, national security expert Richard Fontaine, and former Federal Reserve Chair Ben Bernanke. Trustees are independent of the company’s management and investors.

Since Claude Security entered public beta in April, thousands of organizations have used it to find over a million vulnerabilities.

Instead of waiting for someone to start a scan, Claude Security now keeps up with your repositories as your code changes, keeps track of which findings get fixed, and uses what your team tells it about your environment to decide what matters. Claude Security is powered by our full family of models, including Claude Mythos, with no Cyber Verification Program access required.

The latest version of Claude Security is available today in public beta for Claude Enterprise customers. Organizations receive $25,000 in free usage credits each month, for two months. The offer applies to usage through December 31, 2026. You can view full terms in the Help Center.

Continuous monitoring keeps up with your code

A scan captures one moment, and code changes every day. Teams told us they wanted coverage that stays current without anyone having to schedule it.

Create a project, connect your repositories through the Claude GitHub app (including GitHub Enterprise Server) or with an access token from GitLab and other Git providers, and choose the branch and scope for each. Claude runs a deep baseline scan, then scans changes regularly based upon their risk and complexity, so your list of findings stays close to the current state of your code.

A project can hold multiple repositories, so Claude can catch issues that live between services, like a backend that trusts input a client was supposed to validate.

Findings are marked fixed when the fix ships

Most fixes happen outside the tool that found the issue. Claude Security checks open findings against the code that changed and marks them fixed when the fix lands, whether your team fixed it in Claude Code or in a separate process. If Claude Security finds the issue again later, the finding reopens automatically.

Your team’s knowledge shapes the scan

Every environment has controls a scanner can’t see from the code alone. Teams wanted a way to tell Claude Security about those controls, and to look across services that depend on each other. Now, each project has a knowledge base where you can describe how your code is deployed, which security policies apply, and anything a new security engineer on your team would need to know.

Claude Security also generates a threat model from your code that your team can review and edit. Subsequent scans use those threat models to decide what’s worth flagging. Added context also helps Claude Security skip risks your environment already handles.

Severity and exploit paths for every finding

Each finding comes with a severity rating, judged against your project’s threat model, and an explanation of how an attacker could reach the vulnerable code, so teams can fix what’s actually reachable first. Findings can include a diagram of the attack path.

Findings reach your tools, with controls for larger rollouts

The new API lets you integrate Claude Security into your existing workflows. You can list and read projects and findings, resolve or reopen findings, and create and manage projects and their repositories. Users can create a personal access token in Claude Security settings, and it can only see and change what the user can. Webhooks can also notify your systems when a new finding lands.

Claude Security is also available as an MCP connector in Claude.ai and Claude Code. An engineer can pull up a finding, ask Claude about it, start the fix, and mark it resolved in the same session.

New role-based access controls let admins decide who can view projects, triage findings, and create projects. Organizations can open Claude Security to more teams that own the code without giving everyone access to create projects.

Getting started

The latest version of Claude Security is available in public beta for Claude Enterprise customers starting today. Admins can enable it in the admin console and set who on their team can access it.

Use the Getting Started Guide to set up your first project, and visit the Help Center for more details.

Title: How Claude designed protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins
Context: A binder is only the first step to developing an antivenom Our results show binding only against recombinant toxins, which are grown in the lab from each toxin’s gene rather...
Full Text:
Summary: As part of our work experimenting with how Claude can help accelerate drug discovery, we asked an internal research model to design minibinders (small proteins that attach tightly to a target) against scorpion neurotoxins. Claude worked from our prompt and four follow-ups, which we developed in collaboration with the financial investment research firm Citrini Research. Teams at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience experimentally tested 211 designs for binding. Of these, 17 met our criteria. We’re releasing all 211 designs and their data as a resource for the field.

In August, we showed how Claude designed protein minibinders after being given a single prompt. A month before we released those results, a team from Citrini Research had approached us with an interesting question: could Claude (and AI drug discovery more generally) enable a group of motivated nonexperts to tackle a genuine problem in human health? Members of our life science research team set out to answer this, first by brainstorming problems with Claude. We landed on asking for Claude’s help designing novel protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins, with the hope that they could one day be used to develop a scorpion antivenom.

Scorpions sting 1.2 million people or more every year, resulting in more than 3,250 deaths, mostly among children in parts of the world with limited access to medical care. New treatments are expensive to make, and are also unlikely to earn back the cost of developing them. With so little investment, scorpion envenomation has been described as a neglected tropical disease.

We started by giving Claude the same prompt we’d used in our earlier protein-binder study, after modifying it with Citrini.1 Over the next 64 hours, an internal research model, operating within Claude Science, worked mainly autonomously, although we directed its work with four follow-ups. Under our supervision, Claude analyzed the research data, generated the figures, and drafted the final report.

Claude’s design campaign produced 17 protein binders that each bind to one of four scorpion neurotoxins that are known to be dangerous to humans. Throughout the process, Claude generated 318,484 protein designs and selected 180 of them for testing. Our team added 31 more, with Claude’s help. Our partners at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, two contract research organizations (CROs), lab-tested all 211 designs to see if they would bind to the toxins they were designed against, and 17 designs met our criteria for a binder. We have not confirmed whether these binders neutralize scorpion venom in a cellular environment, so we do not claim to have produced an antivenom.

We sent Claude’s work to two outside experts, Susana Vázquez Torres and Timothy P. Jenkins, who said they felt this work was a promising first step. If AI can now design credible binders against several hard-to-target toxins in days and they can be confirmed in the lab within weeks, this could, in theory, speed up discovery for envenomation and other neglected diseases. The challenge, as always, is turning those binders into safe, affordable, and widely accessible drugs.

We share more detail in our technical report, and are making all 211 designs and their data available.

Designing a binder against almost any target no longer seems unrealistic. We can now obtain very tight binders remarkably quickly, and binding itself is no longer the main bottleneck. For venomous animals such as snakes and scorpions, whose bites and stings kill or seriously injure large numbers of people, particularly in underserved regions, the real impact will come from tackling the parts of the therapeutic pipeline that go beyond binding. The challenge is to use these extraordinary tools to develop molecules that can become real drugs, ones that are safe, affordable, and widely accessible.

Susana Vázquez Torres, Postdoctoral Researcher, Structural Biology Programme, Spanish National Cancer Research Centre (CNIO), Madrid, Spain.

Designing de novo binders against five toxins from four species of scorpions

Scorpion venom contains multiple protein neurotoxins. The neurotoxins that are most likely to harm or kill humans attach to sodium channels, large proteins embedded in the membranes of nerve cells that allow them to fire. When sodium channels are disrupted, nerves fire at the wrong time—this releases large amounts of stress chemicals, like adrenaline. In severe cases, this can cause heart failure and excess fluid buildup in the lungs, occasionally resulting in death.

There are some antivenoms available for scorpion stings. They’re generally made using the antibodies of immunized animals, a process that can take months. Venom is milked from thousands of scorpions and used to immunize horses; scientists then purify the resulting antibodies from the horses’ blood. Traditional antivenoms can work when given early, but they’re usually effective for only a small number of neurotoxins. They’re also expensive to produce, and in many regions are costly or in short supply.

De novo design offers a potential solution. A binder is a molecule that attaches tightly to a specific target; antibodies are one natural example. In principle, a binder that targets the part of a neurotoxin that latches onto sodium channels could stop the toxin from reaching the channel. In de novo design, protein binders are generated from scratch against a specific target. These binders are designed computationally and can be optimized for druglike properties such as potency and stability, which could make them easier to supply in regions where stings most often occur.

Our approach was inspired by an earlier effort that designed de novo proteins that neutralized snake neurotoxins and protected mice. To our knowledge, no de novo-designed binders against scorpion neurotoxins have been described.

For this campaign, we chose to target five scorpion-venom neurotoxins across four regions: Mexico (Cn2), Brazil (Ts1), North Africa (AaH I and AaH II), and the Middle East (LqhIII). We also chose to aim the designs at each toxin’s channel-binding site. Claude picked the toxin structures to use for design by searching the Protein Data Bank (PDB) as well as the AlphaFold database (AFDB). For each toxin, it selected five hotspots, specific amino acid positions on the toxin that its binder designs were meant to latch onto.

We were primarily wondering if Claude could design binders against individual toxins. But we were also curious if Claude could design binders that targeted multiple toxins. There’s a practical reason for trying to design multitoxin binders, namely that it would reduce the number of molecules needed for a universal antivenom cocktail—which would be the most cost-effective and regionally neutral treatment. We selected these five scorpion toxins (Cn2, Ts1, AaH I, AaH II, and LqhIII) as a challenging test of multitoxin design: they share one fold for the overall shape of the protein, but any two are only 26% to 62% identical in their amino acid sequences.

To see how far Claude could go, we asked it to design four kinds of binders: binders against each of the five toxins individually; binders that targeted the β-family toxins Ts1 and Cn2; binders that targeted the α-family toxins AaH II, AaH I, and LqhIII; and binders that targeted all five toxins simultaneously.

Designing credible binders against five toxins in parallel, in a matter of days, is a great showcase of the AI-driven paradigm shift we are seeing in therapeutic discovery. This is especially true for neglected diseases such as animal envenomings, which have been largely starved of innovation due to low commercial incentives. Being able to agentically tackle the uniquely broad target space across animal toxins provides a significant speed-up in discovery, and brings realistic therapeutic solutions much closer.

Timothy P. Jenkins, Associate Professor, Technical University of Denmark.

Claude ran the design campaign with considerable autonomy

Our initial prompt defined the neurotoxin targets, the protein design and folding tools, and the rules for novelty, scoring, and filtering. Beyond choosing the structures and amino acid hotspots, Claude also set the quality thresholds a design had to clear, decided how much to lean on each available design tool, and developed the strategies for designing binders against multiple toxins.

Ultimately, Claude used 12 design tools to generate 318,484 designs, filtering out any that resembled a toxin or a known protein. Claude co-folded and screened 553,052 design-toxin pairs, predicting each pair’s structure as one complex. Sixty-four hours after we gave Claude our initial prompt, it produced its final list of 180 designs. The campaign used on the order of 10,000 GPU hours.2

Claude worked autonomously for 24 hours following our first prompt. Its results encouraged us to prompt Claude to continue its campaign and look for better designs. Our follow-up prompts were mainly focused on directing Claude to design a multitoxin binder. Claude selected most of the 180 designs—including our strongest binder (Cn2-B1)—only after our third follow-up. At our request, Claude sent the protein sequences to Twist Bioscience (in emails indicating they were written by Claude), which produced the proteins in order to see how well they would bind to the toxins. We later worked with Claude to add another 31 designs, increasing the total to 211 designs: 60 designs against a single toxin (12 per toxin), 30 designs against the two β-family toxins, 30 designs against the three α-family toxins, and 91 designs against all five toxins.

Of the 211 designs our teams assessed, 17 met our criteria for a binder, each against a single toxin. None of the designs made against multiple toxins met our criteria for more than one. (Beyond being limited by its current capabilities, there could be many explanations for why Claude struggled with this, including our prompting, the limitations of available design tools, and even the biological feasibility of multitoxin design.) Seven designs were binders against Cn2, four against AaH II, four against AaH I, and two against LqhIII. Among the 60 single-toxin designs, 11 were binders (18%). This rate is consistent with typical protein design campaigns, including our previous work.

Testing Claude's designs in the lab

After completing the campaign, we sent the designs to Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience to test them for binding. Each group produced the designs in their labs, but in different formats. Adaptyv Bio expressed them in a cell-free system, which uses protein-making machinery extracted from bacteria rather than living cells. Twist Bioscience expressed the designs in mammalian cells (in this case, human kidney cells) as fusions to Fc, the stem of an antibody. These are complementary ways to measure the underlying binding process, and we combined them in order to improve confidence in our results.

Both labs measured binding by surface plasmon resonance (SPR), in which a toxin flows over the design while the SPR instrument tracks in real time how quickly a toxin binds to and detaches from it. The resulting trace, called a sensorgram, produces a measurement known as the dissociation constant (KD), which is a measurement for binding strength (or affinity). The lower the KD, the tighter the binding.

When it came to evaluating the resulting designs, we set out strict criteria for labeling a design a binder against a toxin. The design needed to be a hit at both labs3—that is, it needed to show evidence of binding against that toxin in every replicate, and every KD needed to be 1 µM or tighter. We also required that the design show no signal against CLEC12A, an unrelated human protein used to measure off-target binding or “stickiness.”

Claude’s Cn2 binders likely bind the same site as a toxin-neutralizing antibody

Antibodies and nanobodies remain the standard for de novo designs to beat. Three such molecules have reported affinities (KD) below 1 nM (nanomolar) against Cn2 or AaH II, and they have been shown to protect mice from scorpion toxins.

Our two strongest binders, which we call Cn2-B1 and Cn2-B2, target Cn2, a neurotoxin from the Mexican scorpion Centruroides noxius. They each bound Cn2 tightly at both Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, with affinities (KD) in the single-digit nanomolar range.

One way to find out whether two molecules (e.g., an antibody and a miniprotein) bind the same site on a target is with a competition experiment, which tests whether both binders can attach to the target at the same time. If the presence of one molecule reduces the other molecule’s binding, then they likely compete for the same binding site.

Our competition experiments suggest our Cn2 binders each attach on or near the same epitope (binding site) as an antibody called LR, which has been reported to neutralize Cn2 in mice. LR’s binding site covers the part of Cn2 that attaches to the sodium channel and causes nerves to misfire. We have not tested our strongest binders, Cn2-B1 and Cn2-B2, in a cellular environment or in live animals, but the fact that they compete with LR suggests that they will likely neutralize Cn2.

A binder is only the first step to developing an antivenom

Our results show binding only against recombinant toxins, which are grown in the lab from each toxin’s gene rather than purified from venom. The two biggest limitations of this study are that we didn’t test any design for neutralization in vitro (against cells grown in the lab) or for efficacy in vivo (in living animals, such as mice).

If we were to advance one design toward a therapy, Cn2-B1 would be one of our strongest candidates. First, though, we would need to confirm the design also binds toxin purified from venom. We would then assess it for function in vitro with patch-clamp recordings (which can measure the electrical current passing through sodium channels) to see whether it stops the toxin from acting on the channel. Then, we would need to test the binder in mice to see whether it actually protects them. Beyond neutralizing the toxin, a treatment must also be safe, stable, affordable, and available where stings occur. Reaching patients will also take cooperation from clinicians, funders, and policymakers.

We are releasing all 211 designs and their binding data so that other researchers can build on our work. We hope this demonstration of Claude’s capabilities, along with the data we are releasing, will help accelerate further research into antivenom design.

Further reading

The following resources provide further technical depth and more detailed information about the results described above:

Technical report;

Data release: all 211 designs, their predicted structures and scores, and experimental data;

Our previous posts on protein design and uplifting biomolecular modeling.
