Title: Using Claude to reduce the attack surface of code
Context: Showing how previously unknown vulnerabilities might be exploited is, however, only the start of what frontier AI models can do for cyber defense
Full Text:
Chris Rohlf

Over the past year, we’ve published lots of data that shows that frontier AI models are more than capable of discovering and exploiting security vulnerabilities. Showing how previously unknown vulnerabilities might be exploited is, however, only the start of what frontier AI models can do for cyber defense. In this post, we summarize some of our initial research into automated attack surface analysis and reduction: the process of using AI models to map the code that is reachable, then removing or restricting access to anything than a given deployment doesn’t need to expose.

Automated attack surface analysis and reduction can meaningfully improve the security of deployed software in the near term. Securing software by finding and fixing individual vulnerabilities alone scales poorly: fixing even a critical vulnerability tells you nothing about the vulnerabilities that remain. By contrast, reducing code reachability can reduce the severity of unknown vulnerabilities, including the ones that might be under active exploitation. These techniques don’t remove the unknown vulnerabilities in the code, but they do make the vulnerabilities harder to reach, and thereby reduce their severity. Minimizing codebases’ attack surface results in better security without ever having to find or fix an individual vulnerability.

Below, we preview some of the data we’ve collected from applying attack surface reduction techniques to large open-source codebases using Claude. Our aim in doing so is to show that Claude can meaningfully, and economically, improve software security through the methods we outline. Specifically, we ran Claude over 25 projects (in a variety of languages), and it discovered 493 issues. With these results in mind, we discuss how developers can apply similar techniques to their own code.

Methods for reducing codebases’ attack surface

Over time, software has a tendency to become more complicated, with new layers of abstractions, new dependencies, and new features slowly piling on top of one-another. This can often cause it to function very differently to how its original developers intended. And it is a big part of why attackers are often so successful: they study exactly how a piece of code behaves in practice, rather than how its developers intended or designed it to work.

Automated attack surface analysis and reduction techniques aim to discover unnecessary attack surfaces, then move that code behind an appropriate gate. This might involve moving code from pre-authentication to post-authentication, from 0-click to 1-click, from on-by-default to explicit opt-in, or from the first message of a protocol to deeper in the session state machine. Some code is meant to be reachable before these stages, but a lot it is not, and, given the complexity that comes with code churn across thousands or millions of lines of code, unnecessary exposure of features often goes unnoticed.

There are numerous ways to reduce the attack surface of code. In our own research efforts, we focused on three methods in particular:

Default configuration. We identified code that was reachable in its shipped default configuration but wasn’t intended to be used by any default functionality.

Configuration interaction. We found pairs of options that looked reasonable on their own, but which caused issues when configured together (for instance, by silently disabling a security control, or leaving a features behavior undefined while its code remains reachable).

Early reachability. We identified security sensitive and complex code that runs either before an appropriate security control (such as authentication), without victim interaction, or before a protocol state transition.

We wanted to understand how well Claude could take these three descriptions of attack surface and discover real issues in large and complex codebases. We analyzed 25 open source projects (representing over five million lines of code), written in languages including C, C++, Java, PHP, and Python. Claude created an inventory of over 17,000 configuration options across these projects. Of those, 3,842 related to the configuration of a control or feature that was security relevant.

For the purposes of our research, we broke down these open source projects into three broad categories:

Public. These projects are built to serve any user who can reach them, or to consume data authored by parties they cannot identify. (Examples include a DNS resolver parsing upstream answers, or a proxy parsing origin responses.)

Gated. These projects are intended to serve authenticated users (such as those with a password, key or certificate holders, or enrolled devices). The software still allows for arbitrary client requests, but no functionality is available until the user has been authenticated.

Private. These are built and deployed to serve the operator's own private environment. In these cases, adding a control like an authentication layer is optional, but outside the scope of the software.

These categories help to contextualize our results. For example, we’d expect a significant percentage of a Public codebase to be reachable in the default configuration (since it’s designed to serve any user), but the opposite to be true for projects in the Gated category.

Claude’s findings

Claude found 493 issues using the three methods described above. Several themes stuck out to us from its results.

First, Claude found that all eleven gated projects had code that was unintentionally reachable (although this code wasn’t a significant percentage of the total lines of code for any of those projects). Specifically, Claude discovered 93 unnecessary pre-authentication surfaces in the default configuration of the gated cohort, 37 locations where code executed, or state was recorded, before authentication, and 61 configuration combinations that silently weakened a pre-authentication control configured by the administrator. None of these issues would have been immediately exploitable on their own, but they create a much larger attack surface than is necessary.

Second, Claude’s work mitigating configuration interaction issues produced some of the most interesting and impactful findings (across all project types). Claude found 162 security sensitive configuration combinations that were accepted both without an error or warning and without any documentation of the expected behavior of their interaction. In 94 of those cases, the combination silently turned off a security control. The other 68 cases were inconsistencies in the same security mechanisms (e.g. a listener or login path would remain reachable even though the configuration would say it was disabled; two settings would conflict, and the one that would take precedence would depend on their order in the configuration file, or a protection configured by the administrator would do nothing while its code remained reachable). While some of these configuration combinations might be non-standard or infrequently used, there would be nothing preventing an administrator of these projects from configuring and deploying the code in this way.

Claude also found one specific pattern that turned up independently in four unrelated projects. This would work as follows. An administrator would write an access rule for remote clients using a hostname or a wildcard pattern, instead of an IP address. When a client connects, the server would compare that rule against the client’s hostname. Whether the server ever learned that hostname would depend on a separate option that controlled reverse DNS lookups (which most projects had configured off). With lookups off, the server would only have the client’s IP address. The server would compare the rule against that address as plain text. But a hostname pattern can never match an IP address. This means that a deny rule would never fire, and the list would fail open. Some of the affected projects mention in their documentation that hostname rules depend on DNS lookups being enabled, but none state that a deny list written this way would have fail open behavior.

Third, Claude often discovered that two configuration options would conflict in a way that silently dropped a security check. In one case, an administrator could require every connecting client to prove its identity with a certificate. In another, the code was only intended to delay that check until it was required, but in fact disabled the check entirely. A server that was configured to accept only trusted clients would therefore accept a connection from anyone. This exposed a large body of request handling code (which was supposed to be behind the certificate check) to unauthenticated clients. The software accepted both configuration options together with no warning under default settings; the documentation never mentioned that the certificate requirement had been dropped. This conflicting set of configuration options had been present in the software for 21 years.

Finally, Claude discovered an issue in a project that left authentication off by default (and expected the administrator to turn it on). The option that required TLS client certificates was honored on most of the project’s network endpoints, but silently ignored on a few others (ones which loaded their TLS settings through a path with a different namespace). This meant that a client with no certificate could complete the TLS handshake and open a session on an affected endpoint. Nothing would be logged about the ignored setting. Whether the option takes effect would depend on the namespace used by the administrator in the configuration. One form of the setting name works on every endpoint, but the shorter form—which most examples use—is dropped on the affected ones.

Case study: OpenSSH

Surprisingly, when measured as a percentage of the total lines of code, the project for which Claude achieved the largest reduction in attack surface was OpenSSH. OpenSSH is a high quality C codebase that provides secure remote access. Claude traced the input paths of the SSH daemon in the 10.4 release and found roughly 4,500 lines of new and experimental code for ML-DSA-44, a post-quantum signature algorithm, that an unauthenticated client could reach in the default configuration. ML-DSA is not enabled by default, but the code was reachable regardless, even when an administrator explicitly excluded the algorithm. The daemon parsed whichever key type the client sent, (and, for certificates, it also verified the embedded CA signature). Only then did it check whether that key type was allowed. There is no good reason for this complex, memory unsafe code to be reachable when it hasn’t been enabled by the configuration. Those 4,500 lines of code in ML-DSA-44 are about 16% of OpenSSH’s own pre-authentication code in a default sshd. We reported this to the OpenSSH developers along with patches. The 10.5 release moved the check before parsing.

Claude then noted two gaps in the 10.5 check. The first was a mismatch between what the client claimed and what it sent. The check looked at the algorithm name advertised by the client, but the parser was chosen by a type string embedded inside the key blob. A client could advertise ssh-ed25519, pass the check, and still send an ML-DSA key that would be parsed.

The second gap was in the 10.5 check’s certificates. Certificate key types were enabled by default. Given a certificate supplied by an attacker, sshd would deserialize the embedded CA public key and run a full signature verification with it, for any supported algorithm, before consulting the configuration. The user key signature path was properly gated behind the list of public keys allowed to connect to the server, but the CA signature path was not. That made every public key signature verifier in the binary reachable by any client that could complete a key exchange. We built a proof of concept and worked through several iterations of a fix with the maintainers. The resulting change placed the checks inside the parser itself. The encoded key type and the certificate’s CA signature algorithm are now compared against the configured allow lists before the corresponding deserialization or signature verification.

This fix removed roughly a fifth of the OpenSSH code that an unauthenticated client previously could have reached in a default build. Almost all of that was the new ML-DSA code, which is now unreachable even for a client that lies about its key type or hides an ML-DSA CA key inside an otherwise acceptable certificate. Certificates signed with an allowed CA algorithm are still parsed and verified, but the check now runs before parsing. The maintainers shipped the changes described here in version 10.6.

OpenSSH is some of the most heavily audited code in the world. If unnecessary reachability survives there, it can survive anywhere. This suggests that reducing the attack surface of codebases is likely to pay dividends across many important codebases.

Conclusion

It is perhaps impossible to measure how many unknown vulnerabilities are in any given codebase. And there is plenty of data that shows attackers can and will find those vulnerabilities with enough time (particularly if equipped with frontier AI models). But a defender who reduces unnecessary attack surface in their code reduces the risk from all of the unknown vulnerabilities in that code at once—including any that are already being quietly exploited. OpenSSH is some of the most audited C code in the world. Yet it shipped around 4,500 lines of experimental signature parsing code that could have been reached by an attacker prior to any configuration check.

We have combined the attack surface reduction techniques we described above into one reusable Claude skill, which we are working to integrate into OSS-Scanner. The skill runs three passes on a codebase. Each time it starts fresh (with an empty context window), except for a short piece of context it receives from the prior pass.

In the first pass, the skill looks at whether there is code that the default configuration allows to be reached but which isn’t used by any intended functionality. In the second pass, it looks at the code that runs before any hard gates (like authentication) or before protocol state machine entry points, in any configuration. Finally, third, the skill assesses which combinations of configurations silently switch a security control off or degrade its efficacy. In every pass, Claude creates an inventory of the entry points from the code and confirms each finding with a dynamic trace of the program. For default configuration findings, it designs and implements a gate and ensures that this causes no change in the program’s default behavior. It does so by running the project's own test suite (along with a black box regression suite) against the baseline; it requires modified builds to have identical results. Any gate that would change a non-default configuration is set aside for a human to decide. For the other two passes, it proposes changes like reordering a configuration check, adding a guard to enforce state ordering, or rejecting the combination at configuration load. Even without using this specific skill, we think the broad methodology outlined here is likely to be effective.

The techniques outlined in this post offer only a very limited view into what is possible in attack surface reduction. For instance, Claude is also capable of analyzing and comparing runtime logs against configurations to ensure that only required functionality has been enabled: disabling unused parsers, legacy protocols, and dashboards reduces security risk at little cost.

We encourage organizations to explore using Claude to analyze and reduce the attack surface of the software they depend on. We expect this to be one of the most practical ways that developers can measurably improve the security of the code the world already runs on.

Title: OpenCode Breach Could Affect OpenAI, Anthropic and Google
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
A security breach affecting open-source AI agent framework provider OpenCode could expose API keys linked to users of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google AI models.

On October 17, OpenCode confirmed a security breach that occurred the night before and affected its Console service, which allows teams to share access to AI models through centrally managed API credentials.

Rather than exposing the underlying OpenAI, Anthropic or Google keys to individual team members, Console stores each workspace’s credentials and uses them to authenticate requests to the respective providers.

OpenCode is a widely used AI agent platform designed for software developers. It has 217,000 stars on GitHub.

In a July 2026 interview with Y Combinator – financial backer of Anomaly, the company which develops and maintains OpenCode – the founder and CEO Jay V claimed OpenCode had reached approximately 13 million monthly active users and 4.6 million weekly active users.

OpenCode Points to Unauthorized Access to Legacy System

The incident was “related to a large-scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users,” said OpenCode on social media.

“We have notified them all this morning via email. If you did not get an email you were not impacted, it was a subset of users who had external providers linked,” the company added.

The email was made public by several OpenCode users on the dedicated subreddit forum and the official Discord channel.

The email said OpenCode had "identified unauthorized access to a legacy system that we were in the process of decommissioning" and that "third party provider keys (e.g. OpenAI, Anthropic) saved in your workspace may have been exposed."

Specifically, Dax Raad, one of the main contributors to OpenCode and co-founder of Anomaly, noted on X that the breach involved only "the OpenCode Console, not OpenCode itself.”

OpenCode also notified Anthropic, OpenAI and Google to remediate the issue.

Recommended Steps to Mitigate OpenCode Threat

In an incident response report, software supply chain security firm Safeguard provided recommendations for OpenCode users to identify whether they have been affected by the incident and mitigate its impact:

Key steps include:

Checking whether you may be affected: search your inbox for the subject line “Action Required: Potential provider key breach.” If you have received the email, follow the guidance provided. If not, still review your keys as a precaution

Identifying all potentially exposed keys: list every OpenAI, Anthropic and Google Gemini API key that was ever stored in an OpenCode Console workspace, including keys added by other workspace admins

Reviewing API usage for suspicious activity: check each provider’s usage and billing reports from 16 October onward, and further back if possible. Look for unexpected usage spikes, unfamiliar models or unexplained charges

Creating replacement keys: generate new API keys for any potentially exposed credentials before revoking the old ones. Use project- or workspace-specific keys with appropriate restrictions and spending limits

Revoking potentially exposed keys: disable or delete the old keys through the relevant provider dashboard. Do not assume a key is safe simply because it has not shown suspicious usage

Updating all systems using the old keys: replace them in CI/CD secrets, environment files, local agent configurations, production applications, and team members’ machines. Ensure all consumers use the new keys before removing any remaining dependencies on the old ones

Verifying that old keys no longer function: test revoked keys against the relevant provider APIs and confirm they return an authentication error rather than a successful response

Applying additional security controls: restrict keys to the required projects and APIs, set appropriate spending limits and budget alerts, and review workspace access and permissions

Securing your OpenCode Console configuration: if you continue using Console with your own provider credentials, add a dedicated, restricted API key rather than reusing a production key.

OpenCode and Anomaly have been contacted with a request for comment.

Title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
Context: It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-...
Full Text:
At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI.

In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.

In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it.

Growing our monorepo

Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned.

Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard.

As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.

Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load. This bought us time, but they became harder to operate as our merge rate increased. Seeds fell further from the tip of main between refreshes, and it took more and more care to keep operations that depend on history, like diff and blame, working on partial clones.

Taking a step back, we noticed that, like most companies, we were using git as a centralized system with one authoritative copy, but nearly all of our clients were agents and jobs that are online by definition. The properties that make git excellent for distributed, offline work were actively undermining our ability to scale as the repo grew. So we asked ourselves: if we designed source control with the fact that agents are always online in mind from the start, what would it look like?

Principles for agent-scale source control

With agentic coding, many common assumptions about how software is developed are evolving. We embraced these changes when building Scion, which allowed us to take a fundamentally different approach than git on several core principles. Source control for huge monorepos has prior art, notably Google’s Piper and Meta’s Sapling,2 so we were able to build Scion with their hard-won lessons in mind. Our principles are:

Clients are always online. Git assumes that clients work offline and need a complete copy of the repository. Since nearly all of our clients are agents and jobs, we designed Scion’s client and protocols around a server that is always reachable, and have clients fetch data when they need it.

Client-server asymmetry. In git, every client is capable of being a full-fledged server. In Scion, the server answers questions about file history and blame, creates commits, performs merges and rebases, and so on. The client maintains a bounded local object cache, lays out the working copy files on disk, monitors for filesystem changes, and gives users an ergonomic way to work with the server. It can compute very little on its own but, in exchange, it requires much less data locally.

A comprehensive source control service can power many novel applications. With git, a CI job or tool that needs to ask a question about the repository, such as who last changed a line or how two commits are related, has to maintain a local copy of the repo or hope that vendor-specific APIs provide the answer. With Scion, all of the source control queries the client uses are also exposed via API, so in many cases jobs don’t need a local repository at all. Many internal tools, such as our automated bisect and revert pipelines, wouldn’t be practical at scale without this cheap, programmatic access to source control.

Everything must be horizontally scalable. At our peak, we ran several hundred git mirrors, which significantly strained capacity and no longer scaled once the repo outgrew the mirrors’ disks or memory limits. In Scion, the repository’s data is distributed, and every component is independently scalable; there is no fully materialized copy of the repo anywhere, even on the server. There is no equivalent of packfiles (git’s compressed bundles of objects), so no repository maintenance is needed.

Commits must be cheap, incremental, and lock-free. In git, you commit locally and then push to share your work. In Scion, every commit, rebase, or merge happens on the server, so there’s nothing to push, but each of those operations needs to be fast. The cost of creating a commit and updating its downstream data structures has to scale with the size of the change, not the overall size of the repo, or the server can’t keep up. The development lifecycle in Scion discourages refs (pointers to commits, such as branches and tags), except for the main ref or release branches, because global state that every server has to agree on is a looming scaling problem.

The working copy is optional, and sparse by design. Because our monorepo is so large, and because we check out code tens of millions of times a day for CI, we wanted to avoid checkouts whenever we could. With Scion, a CI job that needs the diff between a commit and its merge base, for example, can ask the server for it. The same goes for writes: many write workloads can also skip the checkout and function entirely via API. Scion’s protocol is centered around sparse checkouts, which only contain the directories the client asks for, and virtualized checkouts, which materialize files on demand, so when a job does need files on disk, the client only pays for what it actually reads.

How Scion works

It’s helpful to understand how these principles came together in practice when building Scion. These insights can apply to other source control systems or, more broadly, to other stages of the software development lifecycle.

Data structures

In Scion, the unit of work is a “changeset,” an entry in a write-ahead log. A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent,1 along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage. Changesets are created server-side and are available everywhere, instantly.

This structure lets us accept changesets with very high throughput because there are no packfiles to accept, no locking or cross-server coordination, and no refs to move around. Scion does technically support refs, but since neither creating nor fetching commits involves them, moving one is a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row that happens separately from creating changesets.

A changeset records only what’s changed, so on its own, it can’t quickly answer questions like who last edited a line or which commits affected a file. To answer those, Scion builds additional data structures from the changesets, including dedicated structures for file blame and path history and skip lists for the commit graph. We call everything that isn’t directly part of the changeset “derived data,” and we compute it all through one generic mechanism. Each type of derived data is defined recursively, so its value for a changeset is computed from its values for that changeset’s parents.

This mechanism has three benefits. First, we can easily add a new type of derived data when a new data structure would make some operation faster. Second, for each type, we can choose whether to compute it eagerly or defer the work, so we avoid materializing data we don’t need. And third, because the client never sees the internals of these data structures, we can optimize them without changing the client. We’ve added new types of derived data many times as the system has grown, such as new indices for performing copy detection or path-based file search.

Scaling Scion

A small fleet of Scion servers provides source control APIs for any operation a client needs, such as getting changesets, computing diffs, finding merge bases, and fetching blobs. All source control data is content-addressed, so a piece of data never changes once it’s stored, and any server can cache it without checking with the others. As a result, the servers are horizontally scalable and require little coordination. They are essentially large caches that can also compute derived data on the fly and write the results back to Spanner.

Scion’s many consumers no longer need to maintain local repositories of their own. Fetching and maintaining the repository used to be a significant maintenance burden for CI jobs or tools that needed to ask source control questions, particularly about commit ancestry and blame. Early in the migration, before we had our own client, repo format, or protocols, Scion only answered these “metadata” queries. Fetching file contents and materializing working copies are far more data-intensive operations, and they needed a design of their own.

Scion’s scn client deviates from git’s fetch protocols in several important ways and, as a result, lends itself to a highly scalable architecture that requires significantly less CPU than git servers. Scion’s negotiation doesn’t tell the server what the client already has; instead, it operates exclusively on trees and blobs the client wants. Starting from a root tree, the client checks its local store for missing trees and requests them recursively, then repeats the process for blobs. Every request is for a specific object that never changes, so any cache can answer it, and the architecture closely resembles traditional tiered caches. The process is also efficient and resumable, because there is no single multi-gigabyte packfile response. Sparse and even virtualized checkouts don’t need special support, because the client simply doesn’t ask for trees it doesn’t want.

In the fleet, the client talks over a socket to a daemon, scion-daemon, that stores objects for the whole node. Most of our nodes need access to the monorepo, and jobs on the same node reuse most of the same objects. Each daemon starts from a periodically refreshed snapshot, then talks only to the tree and blob cache servers in its region, called scion-cache. These cache servers stream objects directly from memory, in the disk format that the daemon will consume, so they don’t need to spend time computing the client’s missing objects or performing delta compression. When a cache is missing an object, it asks the authoritative scion-servers, which read from Spanner or cloud storage as needed.

The scion-daemon, scion-cache, and scion-server all respond to identical RPCs for this protocol, so the client doesn’t need to know the cache topology. Any tier could theoretically talk to any other, but we strictly enforce the tiering to isolate failure domains. We want to avoid a situation where a failure in a regional scion-cache overwhelms the upstream scion-servers and brings down the entire system.

Each tier of this system maintains a cache hit rate of over 99% and does not require long-lived state, so it’s easy to scale up if needed. Our Scion infrastructure footprint is now 200x smaller than our previous git mirroring infrastructure in terms of CPU and memory requirements. CI and research jobs check out code two orders of magnitude faster (in seconds rather than minutes), which frees up a sizable amount of capacity across the fleet; CI alone realized a 25% CPU capacity win. Neither clients nor caches need to perform repository maintenance, which simplifies the lifecycle management of our jobs.

What we learned building Scion

We started building Scion around the same time as Claude Mythos Preview and Claude Tag became available internally. Both of these releases simultaneously amplified the need for Scion and meaningfully accelerated how quickly we could build it.

Here’s a particularly striking example. Earlier in the year, we had largely handwritten the first version of the git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline as a prototype. We thought it was good—until we got our hands on an early internal snapshot of Claude Mythos Preview. We asked it to rewrite the whole thing, and with no further instructions, it produced a version that consumed 20x less memory and was 4x faster, while preserving all of the implicit invariants around ingestion ordering and data structures.

What we learned building and operating Scion offers some interesting lessons for what building agent-scale software could look like.

Rapid development with a small team will become more common. A team of seven people built both Scion and Antique (our code review tool, which we could easily write a whole other blog post about), not to mention half a dozen related systems, and fully migrated to them in five months. We did all this while the volume of code merged per day increased by 10x. In the past, developing and deploying a source control system like this would have taken a company years of iterative migration, with many more engineers. We think this sort of fast, nimble migration will become more common in the future.

Engineers are no less valuable, but their work is changing. All of the engineers who worked on this system would now rate Claude as better at writing code than them. But our engineers still supplied the invaluable understanding of the high-level inter-system components and the design-level tradeoffs, making informed choices around the problems we wanted to solve and the scale we knew we needed to achieve. Very often, we found that the role of the engineers was to tell Claude “no.” Agents will sometimes violate core system constraints to satisfy a pattern that should never have been allowed in the first place. This was particularly common in our migration. For example, there were multiple systems that tried to brute force looking up when a change merged to main by linearly reading the commit log instead of asking our code review tool. Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. For example, one such review was overly defensive about trusting another internal service, which resulted in Claude adding excessive validation and complexity. Our team members still review every change request for the system, but they now examine the intent of the change as opposed to reading every line of code.

We were able to substantially improve optimization and quality. By virtue of Claude’s ability to write immense amounts of code much faster than we could ourselves, Scion is among the most well-tested and well-defended codebases we have ever worked on. Even on our tight timeline, we were able to build hermetic simulations of every non-trivial infrastructure and source control interaction we’ve ever encountered, as well as fuzzing and sophisticated rate limiting. Claude also casually found significant optimizations—for example, an algorithmic optimization to ancestry queries that missed one of our indexes—that would have taken an expert days or weeks of analysis and tuning… and then did it all again the next day.

We laid the groundwork for new forms of monorepo security. Managing safety, security, and compliance in a massive monorepo is as important as managing the size and scale. We built Scion with these in mind from the start. It supports rich access control on repositories, as well as the ability to apply permissions to individual directories in order to protect the most sensitive code without losing the benefits of a monorepo. Furthermore, the code review tooling we built can express complex semantic constraints on approvals, which lets us differentiate simple things like comment-only changes from sensitive logical changes, so that human reviewers can focus on the most consequential changes.

A new level of operational excellence is possible. Our team uses Claude Tag heavily, which has helped us monitor each component of the system. For example, we created Slack channels where we tasked Claude with being obsessively focused on the health of a single component. We call these Claudes “superfans.” We have a scion-daemon superfan, a scion-cache superfan, an Antique merge queue superfan, and so on. They have access to our telemetry and logs, and act like an experienced engineer who has nothing better to do than to refresh charts and look for anything strange. We also have traditional alerts for all of our systems, but our superfans can detect subtle and novel issues that make these alerts seem one-dimensional by comparison.

We’re completely rethinking our priors. This project prompted us to take a very hard look at other workflows designed for human scale. A proper merge queue, for example, doesn’t make much sense at agent scale. What does CI even mean when hundreds or even thousands of changes can merge while tests are running? We haven’t been able to effectively replicate the industry standard of a global repository lock on the merge queue, so instead, we’ve invested in post-merge and pre-deploy automated testing. This does mean that concurrent changes can conflict, but Claude can typically fix these conflicts faster than humans can even identify them.

Contributing to the wider ecosystem

We see Scion as just one part of the answer to the scaling concerns that increasingly capable AI agents have raised. We’re sharing these details as an example of how teams can tackle similar challenges, though we don’t expect our solution, or our considerations, to suit every case.

Scion is by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use. The concepts we’ve outlined here really only make sense for truly enormous monorepos, with either tens of thousands of engineers or swarms of agents prolifically writing code. Plus, Anthropic is unique in that our ability to spend tokens for internal use far exceeds what any other business would realistically want to spend. We do this both to address our own software development needs, and to test Claude’s capabilities.

Practically speaking, it’s difficult to offer Scion in a form that would be broadly useful to other organizations. It diverges significantly from git, meaning companies would need to migrate every piece of the development lifecycle, and it requires its own code review, code search, and CI. Our internal versions of these components are highly bespoke, so they would be difficult for other organizations to adopt, and we worry that attempting to build a public version that tries to please everyone wouldn’t actually be very useful.

However, we anticipate that this class of problems will become more commonplace over the next six to 12 months, and it would be an inefficient use of engineering resources for every company using git to face similar challenges alone. Given that, we think the most impactful thing we can do is to share our thinking, so that other developers can apply some of the most successful parts of Scion to git without departing from the overall model. A git server doesn’t have to work the same way as a git client does; novel server architectures exist that provide significant scaling improvements. Git platforms can provide comprehensive server-side RPCs like Scion, perhaps even in a standardized way across forges that the git client can learn to talk to. The negotiation protocol doesn’t have to look exactly like it does today, either, and the various sparse and shallow features in git can be made to compose well.

Lastly, we want to acknowledge that the git community has spent nearly two decades scaling the platform for millions of developers. Our contribution is far narrower: sharing our early view into how agentic software development interacts with these systems, so that we can partner with GitHub, GitLab, and the OSS community to support the changing needs of developers. We’re all in it together as the software development lifecycle intersects with the AI exponential.

Title: How employment is changing at Anthropic
Context: A defining feature of working in an AI-heavy organization is constant pressure to streamline oneself out of this bottleneck position when possible
Full Text:
Nathan Wilmers, Regina Catipon, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory

How has AI restructured work and employment at Anthropic? As a company at the frontier of AI adoption, Anthropic could be a leading indicator of how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy.

Key findings

Anthropic has been hiring for a smaller share of junior technical positions. This occurred as hours worked by AI agents relative to employees rapidly expanded. By August interactive AI agent hours outnumbered employees’ six to one.

As AI agents diffused through the company, Anthropic began producing more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts. Following the same employee over time, output rose as they adopted new AI tools.

This acceleration makes human attention the bottleneck for agent output. Even among non-technical employees, reading all the output of their Claude agents would take half their work week. In response, employees turn to “meta-work,” of building visibility tools and monitoring agent pipelines.

Changes in work organization are reflected in shifting priorities among hiring managers, who increasingly emphasize autonomy and judgment, relative to technical domain expertise and implementation.

Introduction

What transformations of work and employment can we expect under increasingly powerful AI? Anthropic is worth studying because it has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI. Agents flit through Slack chats and schedule meetings. They autonomously fix bugs and collectively tackle huge engineering projects. Agent hours worked outnumber human hours 6 to 1. Changes happening at Anthropic now give advanced signals about a possible future of work and employment.

This report draws on comprehensive internal Anthropic data covering employment, AI use, output metrics, employee surveys, internal communication patterns, employee calendar data, and hiring decision records. It contextualizes these quantitative data with 17 employee interviews.

We find that even as the company grows, relative hiring in junior technical positions has slowed. Productivity for both engineers and non-technical employees has leapt up and did so sharply when they adopted coding agents. Hiring managers increasingly emphasize applicants’ autonomy and judgment relative to specific technical expertise. A defining feature of working in an AI-heavy organization is constant pressure to streamline oneself out of this bottleneck position when possible. One engineer described work as facing “an army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention.” Employees at Anthropic remain critical. But the nature of their contributions has changed.

Anthropic has responded to these changes by setting up an early warning system to track jobs at risk of disruption, and as jobs evolve the company has prioritized internal redeployments. These actions, taken at the frontier of both AI development and workplace change, show how specific organizational commitments can shape the impact of AI on employment. But they also raise difficult questions about exactly what those commitments should be.

Labor demand at the frontier

Anthropic has expanded rapidly. But it has hired less per dollar of revenue than an earlier generation of large tech companies. At five years old, Anthropic takes in between 2–4 times as much revenue per employee as Meta and Google as they crested in their own rapid growth.1

What jobs are missing? Within Anthropic, discussion of a decline in demand for junior technical employees emerged in core technical functions in January 2026. The teams that relied most heavily on Claude in their own work found that writing code and finding bugs could increasingly be offloaded to Claude. Newly capable models accelerated this perception: “the thing that raised eyebrows was the uplift for performance engineers in particular and it basically overnight changed what we were looking for.”

By April, engineering and research teams had deemphasized hiring for lower band technical positions. When surveyed in the same month, a majority of managers described hiring for a different set of skills due to AI. Around a third of ML and a fifth of SWE managers reported hiring less due to AI.

The shift in employment shares is striking. Figure 1 shows that the share of junior-level employees in technical departments at Anthropic slipped from 21% to 14% since early 2025. The proportion of junior technical hires fell even faster, from 27% to 9%. Postings for juniors have fallen particularly sharply since December 2025.

At the same time, the overall employment share of technical departments within Anthropic has fallen, from 61% to 56% in the last year. As the company expands, technical hiring has continued growing in absolute terms, but intensive hiring in sales, finance, and recruiting has outpaced it. Part of this shift is the natural expansion of business functions as the company scales. Part could reflect coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves. For example, a sales representative designed a custom dashboard and pipeline tailored to their work: “a build like this was out of my wheelhouse, especially with the UI, connecting all the tools, the MCPs. But I built this probably in three to four hours, just iterating on it.” Coding-focused AI agent sessions for non-technical employees (identified as those with no code commits at baseline, excluding new hires) leapt from 2 per month in August 2025 to 90 in May 2026.

Yet this shift in hiring composition is not only a story about automated coding allowing it to diffuse to other domain experts. Within technical departments, the share of employees not actively coding (defined as those making no code commits in the prior 30 days) fell by almost half over the year through April 2026. Part of this is due to a thinning share of non-engineers: the ratio of engineers to product managers, for example, sits at around 17 to 1 and has increased since 2025. The number of commits from managers has also doubled. The supervising and coordinating roles within technical teams increasingly involve building and shipping code.

One area in which non-technical hiring has not accelerated is in the administrative functions that typically scale with a company’s size. A combination of agent assistants, automated review and ticket service outsourcing has left Anthropic clerical-light even as it has grown rapidly. A financial manager built a purchase request review agent and explained to colleagues “it's just trying to find the things that take a lot of hours so they can focus on the other stuff.”

Even clerical work tightly connected to in-person interaction has grown slowly. An executive assistant, who built a personal assistant agent for scheduling and email triage, explained: “I think we've already moved past the point of Claude augmenting away the really entry-level admin type role,” and instead focused their work on higher-order “chief of staff” tasks.

These changes have already involved reallocation: employees working at the company for at least a year were 50% more likely to move across departments each month in 2026 than they were in 2025. Whole teams have also been reallocated as they handed off their work to agents. Consider one product design team, which wrote content like the greetings on Claude.ai: “Hello night owl;” “Coffee and Claude time?” In spring 2026, the team developed a context graph that effectively guided agents to write compelling product content. This “scaled the team out,” its manager explained, but also raised the question of what was left for human writers. The team then rotated into agent prompting and began writing model evals and prompts for Claude. “Writers who used language to drive human behavior are now using it to drive Claude behavior.”

Is AI driving productivity increases at Anthropic?

Are these shifts attributable to AI? At Anthropic, humans are a thin layer atop a growing contingent of AI agents. Based on agent session telemetry, in March 2026, the sum of autonomous and interactive agent work hours leapt past human work hours for the first time. Part of this is fleets of agents conducting industrial-scale software engineering, filling in myriad routine tests and checks, conducting maintenance on a growing mass of infrastructure code, and driving concerted campaigns to translate massive codebases. But even narrowing in on the agents deployed by individual employees, as in Figure 2, by August the agents worked 6 times as many hours as their human handlers.

Anthropic is a software producer, and the vast bulk of tokens flowing through these agents is spent producing software code. Dashboards monitor fleets of agents operating across the company. But personal assistant agents also monitor employee calendars and messages, scheduling, sending to-do lists accumulated from incoming messages, and automatically briefing employees on the people and purpose of their upcoming meetings. Tokens touch a growing range of everyday work tasks.

What do all of these tokens amount to? Figure 3 plots output over time for a range of job functions with measurable output. Consistent with prior reports surveying Anthropic engineers and describing automation of model training and research, code commits per engineer have risen the fastest, coming in at 5x their velocity as six months ago. Data scientists are also querying the growing mass of Anthropic data more, asking Claude agents to get real-time metrics to dashboards and decisionmakers. But Figure 3 shows that even non-technical employees saw output rise as coding agents diffused: lawyers processed more contracts; accounts payable ushered through invoices; salespeople closed more deals.

But is all of this due to Claude usage? During this same period, the company saw explosive business growth. It is easier to close deals when you sell a strong model. To assess the independent effect of AI, we compare the output of employees who adopt agentic coding tools to those who have not yet adopted the tools. This lets us compare employees working in the same month at the company, and therefore exposed to a similar business context, but approaching it with different tools. Note, however, that tool adoption is not random: if employees on the cusp of driving some big new project decide to tool up for it, for example, this would bias our estimates.

We follow 192 engineers over time as they adopt coding agents, compared to 74 engineers who do not adopt agents during the period studied. Figure 4 shows that in the months following adoption, the amount of code that engineers add rises sharply. More code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact. To test for AI code slop, we study code commits made at Anthropic. We compare code committed by the same employee, in the same month, in the same coding directory, but written by coding agents rather than written directly by the human employee. There are many dimensions of code quality, and AI errors may be harder to identify than human ones. But we find no difference in rates of lines of code subsequently removed or reverted.

Figure 4 also looks at what happens after an engineer adopts their first fully autonomous agent. Those who adopt were already on a steeply upward trajectory compared to non-adopters. This suggests that employees shifting toward fully autonomous agents were already ramping up their output.

Do these patterns go beyond coding, into a broader transformation of knowledge work? Anthropic sales representatives steadily adopted AI agents starting last September. Figure 4 shows that after sales representatives adopt agents, they close deals with more clients. Part of this pattern could be driven by representatives with more sales opportunities selecting into automation. But it could also reflect automation of logging and routine communication. One account executive explained that Claude automations handled email drafting and customer management software integrations, replacing around 20% of their prior work tasks. Another noted that similar automations freed them up to focus on face-to-face time, letting them talk to 30% more of their customers than was previously possible: “anytime you do anything a second time, you're kind of like, okay, how can I use Claude to make it so that I don't have to do it a third time?”

Beyond sales, an Anthropic lawyer built a series of Claude automations to scan risks and opportunities, triage legal questions and take first passes through public-facing copy for legal review. A recruiter used Claude to help with candidate sourcing, tracking applications and an analysis that would have taken “maybe a couple of weeks,” freeing him to redesign outdated interview questions and meet with more applicants.

All of this suggests that as AI capabilities improve, it impacts a wide range of jobs across Anthropic. Descriptively, we see junior employment slowing in jobs that use Claude for the most complex tasks (Figure 5).

Bottlenecks and process: new and old tasks in an AI-intensive workplace

Heavy AI adoption reshapes more than employment and productivity. It also drives continual changes in work processes, generating new tasks and shifting employees’ perceptions of their workplace. One employee described this as the “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything” and another that “things we expect in a week are things that would take three months elsewhere.” An internal employee survey asked whether work processes at Anthropic made respondents as productive as possible: 44% of employees agreed in late 2024; 58% by November 2025 (in April 2026, 75% answered yes, but the question weakened by dropping “as possible”). As of August, employees at Anthropic expected that AI will be able to do 75% of their work by 2030, compared to 28% for other Americans.

These ratcheting productivity expectations are dramatized by the cadence of internal model releases. As soon as a new model is available, Anthropic employees start tackling harder problems in interactive coding agent sessions. We measure this with an automated Claude grader rating deidentified sessions’ task demands based on depth, scope and number of systems implicated. The share of tasks above the 90th percentile of difficulty for the old model rises sharply by around 30% (from 10% to 13% of all tasks) and stays elevated in the weeks following model releases. The easy end of tasks given to agents changes little.

Spiraling agent productivity translates into output pitched across humans’ screens and attention. One engineer compared this to babysitting:

They're like, I need my juice box opened and it's an emergency that my juice box is opened. And that is voiced with the same level of concern as the one who has sliced their finger and is bleeding. [...] When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.

In the April 2026 survey, an open-ended question about how AI has impacted day-to-day work, 27% described productivity gains from Claude tools and 20% described their role shifting from actually doing work to managing Claudes.

Amid this model-driven acceleration, human attention is a constant bottleneck. In interactive, multi-turn sessions, the vast majority of agents’ session time is not spent working at all, but spent waiting. We track idle time by subtracting each agent’s active working time from each interactive session’s total wall-clock time. Claude sessions amount to around 80% idly waiting for human input. As one engineer put it, people are “bottlenecking the agents.”

How much time exactly would be needed to read all of Claude’s output from interactive sessions? For each interactive session, we convert each session’s agent output token to word count, assuming average human reading speed. Figure 6 shows that technical functions have seen the volume of coding agent output leap up over the last six months. But even for non-technical groups, interactive Claude sessions are outputting enough content to take up over half of the work week. The deluge of Claude text needs organizing.

One solution to this deluge is rising automation. But this requires work of a different kind. Written standing instructions for agents grew from a few hundred in July 2025 to 8,500 a year later. One engineer set up an agent chief of staff to triage agent requests. Another wrote a performance review for their Claude team: “Hey, let’s talk about what is and is not working about our communication style.” Recruiters built integrated dashboards with agents surfacing problems and initiating actions. A lawyer shifted their attention from reviewing legal questions to doing “SEO for legal advice, you need to write frameworks that [clients’] agents discover.”

Figure 7 shows that this kind of meta-work leapt from 10% of the average employee’s interactive Claude sessions in fall 2025 to 22% in spring 2026. Much of this rise was due specifically to agent management: writing specs for multi-agent runs, looping one agent to review another’s output, and monitoring pipelines. Across functions, human involvement increasingly abstracted from a particular piece of code or writing to the tooling necessary to get agents to do their tasks effectively.

Despite increases in agent reliability and these significant investments in tooling to supervise them, human trust and accountability remains critical. One employee explained that, increasingly, chasing down bugs “uncovers these organizational or systemic or tech debt things that actually require some amount of human convening and decision-making and governance to solve.” In interview after interview, employees described face-to-face coordination as indispensable. Based on calendar data, the median employee spends 20% more time in meetings than a year ago. Part of this reflects the growth of the company, and a shift toward meeting-intensive non-technical roles. But even among employees in technical individual contributor roles, meeting time is up 16% over the past year. Big-picture strategic questions touch a broad range of leveraged positions, and typically require debate and engagement with others. A break from managing the agents typically looks like jumping into a meeting.

Broadly, both technical and non-technical roles have seen implementation parts of their job automated (writing code, identifying bugs, logging progress, drafting emails). Engineers described becoming leaders and managers of agents; non-technical employees described doing more and more of the strategic parts of their job: “that 20% that was strategic becomes 90% of the job.” But for many non-technical roles, core implementation work is also interpersonal: a sales call, an interview, cross-functional alignment on a complex problem. All of this remains human.

Consider too the Slack channels that provide both the front page and backchannels of Anthropic communication. Agents diffused through Slack and eventually appeared in nearly half of active, public channels. Figure 8 zooms in on the communication network of a single large department, drawing on all public Slack channels that department members interacted through. It links both human and agent participants by whether they participated in a Slack thread. The figure shows the remarkable rise of agents, as orange dots blossom and dominate the network.

Agents appear disproportionately in dedicated channels for Claude-human interactions, rather than messaging a lot in incumbent human channels. The underlying structure and density of human communication changes little. Agents did not replace human interaction, but rather added to it: human threads in this department sustained the same number of human responses, while additionally layering on agent responses. Agents become teams for a single employee, rather than nodes with high connectivity to many employees at once.

As humans work amid a growing fleet of AI agents, they face pressure to shift human work into agent-visible channels. If a decision is made in an in-person meeting, and no notes or report-out appears, agents are missing crucial context for updating their goals and assumptions. An employee explained how having their name on a months-old document about Claude swag meant agents kept bringing requests for t-shirts and mugs, long after their responsibilities had changed. Private work, in unlogged meetings and direct messages, is invisible, confusing and discouraged in an AI-heavy workplace. One researcher described this default toward openness as critical to Anthropic’s thoroughgoing integration of AI: “most organizations do not run that way and I think that's a big shift because leaders have to defend feedback out in the open.” The need to feed AI context requires observability of human work and decisions.

Who will thrive in a workplace like this? Shifts in the content of work at Anthropic also show up as changes in the skills that hiring managers prioritize in hiring decisions. We used an automated coder to process hiring manager interview score cards for thousands of employees hired at Anthropic since 2024. These comments are qualitative reactions by interviewers assessing candidates’ performance. The clearest change is increased emphasis on whether candidates have demonstrated creative use of AI tools. In 2024, hiring managers noted candidates' track record on AI tooling in around 5% of assessments for technical roles, and 7% for non-technical roles. By 2026, these rates had tripled for technical roles and quadrupled for non-technical roles. Hiring managers increasingly focus on whether candidates effectively use AI.

Deeper changes in assessment are also visible. Among interviews for technical candidates, the single biggest increases were in comments on applicants’ autonomy and judgment. Discussion of domain expertise shrank as a share of overall assessment. As one manager explained, “I expect models to continue to be jagged, so for my team I want them to be fungible across domains.” Similarly, for non-technical candidates, customer and mission orientation increased, while discussion of execution skills fell. Increasingly, hiring managers assess applicants based on their judgment and commitment, rather than the domain-specific skills and execution automated by AI tools.

What employers can do

The deep adoption of AI at Anthropic makes it a useful case. As AI diffuses and improves, the organization of work could shift as it has in prior waves of technological change. The railroads gave us the managerial corporation, steam power allowed factories, and personal computers delivered the startup. What new organizations will tool-using, reasoning LLMs require, and what will be our role in them? One possibility is single-person startups, each with a human founder steering swarms of agents to rake in billions in revenue. Another is companies built by AI genius CEOs employing human agents only to wield pipettes and testify before Congress.

Anthropic does not look like either of these. It has tripled in size in the last year. It is no longer a small startup. It has also not ceded executive control to its models. Written Slack debates and in-person meetings steer everything from company strategy to team decisions, with little input from AI agents. Keeping human work visible across the company ensures autonomous agents reason from fresh context. Individual contributors orchestrating teams of agents look more like managers in terms of the knowledge they need and the interdependencies in their work. Working and deciding in the open is critical at an AI-intensive organization.

As employees increasingly see their work as managing teams of Claudes, they spend more time building the tools needed to do this effectively in their own distinctive domains. This experimentation means that employees are continually automating their own tasks away. In some roles, they are increasingly removed from the object-level work that originally built their skills. As agents sprint through workflows, human attention and judgment are a bottleneck that the system strains against. From sales to legal, human employees are expected to do more and different tasks. Roles broaden to include building products, managing agents and tackling the strategic and interpersonal work that remain beyond the scope of the best LLMs.

These changes in the organization and content of work have appeared alongside declining shares of junior technical roles in headcount, hiring, and posting. Hiring managers increasingly focus on applicants’ autonomy and judgment, rather than execution and narrow expertise. Overall, Anthropic’s revenue growth relative to its employment growth has sped past even the rapid early productivity growth of a prior generation of technology companies.

Reading these patterns forward and out across the economy suggests that AI diffusion could risk worker displacement. Prior work also finds that AI-native startups and AI-adopters are flatter and employ fewer entry-level employees. What can we learn from Anthropic about how to manage AI upheavals in a way that serves the humans working around them?

Here we want to proceed carefully. There are many parts of Anthropic’s employment practices that cannot be replicated across the economy.

But three features stand out. First, widespread stock ownership gives employees a strong interest in the company’s success. Of course, this is an easy posture for a company that has seen substantial increases in valuation. For many firms, shared ownership may be insufficient or otherwise undesirable. But it is difficult to imagine a version of pro-worker AI adoption in which workers do not hold a financial stake in successful rollout. If individual contributors are expected to “manage agents,” “make VP-level decisions” and be “their own business line,” as interviewees put it, then aligning their interests with the organization is crucial. The post-World War II union-management settlement forged in the 1950s rested on exactly this kind of bargain: labor unions like the United Auto Workers and the United Steel Workers allowed management prerogative over work reorganization (and even intensification) in return for pay increases tied to productivity increases and to a rich array of benefits. Whatever the new deal between AI-affected employees and their employers, a mechanism to share benefits of adoption is essential. At Anthropic, workers codify their expertise for the machine, see their work routines constantly roiled and disrupted, and have seen a large part of their job become speedreading the output of their AI collaborators. They do not do this for free.

Second, Anthropic is standing up an ongoing early warning system to monitor jobs facing AI-driven transformation. A series of role-level metrics for demand and productivity are read against AI capabilities and use. These aggregate metrics help flag where work is shifting. An early warning system allows the company to start reallocating affected employees to jobs with a skills fit that may be less immediately at risk. As companies across the economy reorient to an accelerated pace of work reorganization, effective systems for guiding internal employee reallocation will become increasingly valuable. Turning to the external labor market to meet every new task demanded by AI advances will be a stronger bottleneck the faster AI advances. In this report, we found increased mobility between departments, changing work content, and employees shifting to new tasks as old ones were automated. Building systems to flexibly reallocate workers internally will be critical for AI-intensive organizations.

This commitment to internal worker reallocation raises important tradeoffs. A well-functioning labor market should shift workers into their most productive positions, whether that is at their current employer or another one. Commitments to reallocate incumbent workers could make employers hesitant to take a risk on hiring new employees. In normal economic conditions, particularly intensely competitive ones, such commitments could be costly.

But prioritizing reallocation forces AI-adopting companies to consider ways that AI can create new tasks for new products and new markets, rather than funneling AI applications into replacing human workers to save on labor costs. This could help employers resist the temptation of ‘so-so’ or ‘inefficient’ automation in which AI or other technologies just barely outcompete human workers: employers replace human workers, imposing substantial social costs in lost income for displaced workers, while delivering minimal productivity benefits.

From what we see in Anthropic, both novel and persistently human tasks remain alongside intensive AI use. Uncertainty about the future set of these tasks should recommend preserving a flexible workforce. As one Anthropic executive noted, “a workforce that is anxiously worried is not a workforce doing its best work.”

None of these actions will prevent powerful AI from disrupting jobs. And indeed none directly address the slowdown in junior hires documented in this report. Employment protections for incumbents will not benefit those not hired to begin with. Private action on the part of employers must come alongside farsighted government policy around retraining and income support. Such policy should be guided by a clear picture of the scale of workplace transformation that AI can bring.
